concepts.title: Covariance and Correlation Matrices
concepts.description: The covariance matrix generalizes scalar variance and pairwise covariance to many dimensions at once, packing every feature's variance and every pair's linear co-movement into one symmetric, positive-semidefinite object that the correlation matrix rescales into a unit-free, directly comparable form.
learningObjectives: Define the covariance matrix as a generalization of scalar variance and covariance, and write its formula in terms of a centered data matrix.
Explain why every covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semi-definite, and what a negative eigenvalue would (impossibly) imply.
Derive the correlation matrix from the covariance matrix by normalizing with feature standard deviations, and explain why correlation is scale-invariant while covariance is not.
Read pairwise feature relationships -- strength, direction, redundancy -- directly off a covariance or correlation matrix.
Compute a covariance matrix by hand and with numpy from a small feature matrix, and verify the result against np.cov.

sections.heading: From Scalar Variance to a Matrix of Variances and Covariances
sections.body:
For a single feature, variance measures how spread out its values are around the mean: Var(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. For two features, covariance measures how they move together: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]: positive when they tend to rise and fall together, negative when one rises as the other falls, near zero when there is no consistent linear relationship. The **covariance matrix** asks that question for every feature against every other feature at once. For p features it is a p-by-p matrix whose entry Sigma[i, j] is Cov(X_i, X_j): the diagonal entries Sigma[i, i] are ordinary variances (a feature's covariance with itself), and the off-diagonal entries are the pairwise covariances.

Given a data matrix X with n rows (samples) and p columns (features), the sample covariance matrix has a clean matrix formula once you center the data by subtracting each column's mean: if X_c is X with its column means subtracted, then Sigma = (X_c^T @ X_c) / (n - 1). This one multiplication computes every pairwise sum of centered products at once: row i of X_c^T dotted with column j of X_c is the sum over all samples of (x_i - mean_i)(x_j - mean_j), and dividing by (n - 1) turns it into the sample covariance of features i and j. Dividing by (n - 1) rather than n is **Bessel's correction**, the same bias correction used for scalar sample variance, applied entrywise.

```python
import numpy as np

# rows = samples, columns = [hours_studied, practice_tests_taken, hours_gaming]
X = np.array([
    [2.0, 1.0, 5.0],
    [3.0, 2.0, 4.0],
    [5.0, 4.0, 2.0],
    [7.0, 5.0, 1.0],
    [8.0, 6.0, 0.5],
])

n = X.shape[0]
X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
cov_manual = (X_centered.T @ X_centered) / (n - 1)
cov_numpy = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)

print(np.allclose(cov_manual, cov_numpy))   # True
print(np.round(cov_numpy, 3))
# [[ 6.5    5.25  -4.875]
#  [ 5.25   4.3   -4.   ]
#  [-4.875 -4.     3.75 ]]
```

Note the `rowvar=False` argument. `np.cov` treats each **row** as a variable and each **column** as an observation, the opposite of the samples-by-features layout used here and throughout scikit-learn. Without `rowvar=False`, a samples-by-features matrix is covaried across the wrong axis and you get a matrix of the wrong shape (5-by-5 here instead of 3-by-3). It raises no error, which makes it a common mistake, and the debugging exercise below reproduces it.

sections.heading: Why Symmetry and Positive Semi-Definiteness Are Not Optional
sections.body:
A covariance matrix is always **symmetric**: Sigma[i, j] = Cov(X_i, X_j) = Cov(X_j, X_i) = Sigma[j, i], because multiplication inside the expectation doesn't care about order. The more consequential property is that a covariance matrix is always **positive semi-definite (PSD)**: for any real vector v, v^T @ Sigma @ v >= 0. This follows from what covariance means. The quantity v^T @ Sigma @ v is Var(v^T X): the variance of the single new feature you get from the linear combination v^T X of the original features. A variance can't be negative, so neither can this quadratic form, for any v.

Consequently every eigenvalue of a covariance matrix is nonnegative. An eigenvalue lambda with eigenvector v would require v^T @ Sigma @ v = lambda * ||v||^2, and a negative lambda would make the left side negative, which was just ruled out. This is the guarantee that lets PCA (a later concept in this module) take a covariance matrix's eigendecomposition and treat every eigenvalue as a variance along some direction -- if covariance matrices could have negative eigenvalues, 'variance along this direction' would sometimes be a negative number, which is meaningless.

The *semi* in positive semi-definite matters too: it permits eigenvalues of exactly zero, which happen whenever some linear combination of your features has zero variance -- a feature that's a constant, a feature that's an exact linear function of others (perfect collinearity), or, in high-dimensional data, whenever you have fewer samples than features (n < p). With n samples in p dimensions, the centered data matrix X_c has rank at most min(n - 1, p), so if p > n - 1, the sample covariance matrix is mathematically guaranteed to be singular -- some directions in feature space never varied in your finite sample, whether or not they would in the population. This is common with high-dimensional embeddings (hundreds of dimensions, sometimes fewer samples than that), and it is why naively inverting a sample covariance matrix, which the next concept relies on, can fail or produce garbage.

sections.heading: The Correlation Matrix: Normalizing Covariance Into a Unit-Free Scale
sections.body:
Covariance has an awkward property: its numeric scale depends on the units the features happen to be measured in. Cov(income_in_dollars, age_in_years) might be in the tens of thousands, while Cov(income_in_thousands_of_dollars, age_in_years) for the same relationship is a thousand times smaller. Only the units changed, not the strength of the relationship. This makes raw covariance values hard to compare across different pairs of features, or across different datasets, at a glance.

The **correlation matrix** fixes this by dividing each covariance by the product of the two features' standard deviations: rho[i, j] = Sigma[i, j] / (sigma_i * sigma_j), where sigma_i = sqrt(Sigma[i, i]). This rescaling turns covariance into the familiar Pearson correlation coefficient. Every entry lands in [-1, 1] and the diagonal is always 1 (a feature correlates perfectly with itself), whatever units the features use. A correlation of 0.99 means the same thing whether the features were measured in dollars and years or in millions of dollars and days, which is why correlation matrices, not covariance matrices, are the usual tool for eyeballing feature relationships in exploratory analysis.

```python
stds = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov_numpy))
corr_manual = cov_numpy / np.outer(stds, stds)
corr_numpy = np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False)

print(np.allclose(corr_manual, corr_numpy))   # True
print(np.round(corr_numpy, 3))
# [[ 1.     0.993 -0.987]
#  [ 0.993  1.    -0.996]
#  [-0.987 -0.996  1.   ]]
```

The correlation matrix is the covariance matrix of the **standardized** features (each rescaled to mean 0 and standard deviation 1): standardizing first or normalizing afterward gives the identical matrix. So 'standardize, then take covariance' and 'take correlation' are the same operation, which matters in the PCA concept later in this module: choosing whether to standardize before PCA is choosing between the covariance matrix and the correlation matrix.

sections.heading: Reading a Covariance or Correlation Matrix, and Its Blind Spot
sections.body:
In the worked example above, hours_studied and practice_tests_taken have a correlation of 0.993 -- essentially redundant information, moving together almost in lockstep, which is a strong signal that a model might not need both as separate features. hours_studied and hours_gaming sit at -0.987 -- a strong, almost mechanical trade-off, unsurprising for two activities competing for the same fixed hours in a day. A near-zero off-diagonal entry, by contrast, would say the two features show no *consistent linear* relationship in this data -- more of one doesn't predict more or less of the other, at least not in a straight-line sense.

That last qualifier, *linear*, is the main caveat on every number in a covariance or correlation matrix, and a counterexample makes it concrete. Correlation and covariance are built from sums of products of deviations from the mean, so they cannot detect a relationship that isn't roughly a straight line.

```python
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 13)
y = x ** 2   # y is a completely deterministic function of x -- maximally dependent

X = np.column_stack([x, y])
corr = np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False)
print(np.round(corr, 4))
# [[1. 0.]
#  [0. 1.]]
print("corr(x, x^2) =", round(corr[0, 1], 4))   # 0.0
```

Here y is a deterministic function of x, knowing x tells you y exactly, and yet the Pearson correlation is 0.0 because the relationship is symmetric and curved: as x rises from -3 to 0, y falls; as x rises from 0 to 3, y rises, and the two trends cancel in the single coefficient. A matrix full of near-zero numbers is evidence against *linear* relationships only, not evidence of statistical independence. Treating 'uncorrelated' as 'unrelated' is a common misreading, especially with the nonlinear, high-dimensional relationships that neural network features routinely encode.

examples.title: Computing a Covariance Matrix by Hand and Cross-Checking with numpy
examples.code:
import numpy as np

# rows = samples, columns = [hours_studied, practice_tests_taken, hours_gaming]
X = np.array([
    [2.0, 1.0, 5.0],
    [3.0, 2.0, 4.0],
    [5.0, 4.0, 2.0],
    [7.0, 5.0, 1.0],
    [8.0, 6.0, 0.5],
])

n = X.shape[0]
X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
cov_manual = (X_centered.T @ X_centered) / (n - 1)
cov_numpy = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)

print(np.allclose(cov_manual, cov_numpy))
print(np.round(cov_numpy, 3))
examples.explanation: `X_centered.T @ X_centered` is a 3-by-3 matrix because it's (features x samples) @ (samples x features); entry [i, j] of that product is the sum, over all 5 samples, of the centered value of feature i times the centered value of feature j, the numerator of the covariance formula for that pair. Dividing the whole matrix by (n - 1) = 4 turns every sum into a sample covariance in one vectorized operation instead of a triple-nested loop over feature pairs and samples. The `rowvar=False` argument tells `np.cov` that columns are variables and rows are observations (the usual machine-learning layout) instead of its default of rows as variables. Without it, a samples-by-features matrix gives a 5-by-5 result instead of 3-by-3, the bug in the debugging exercise below.

examples.title: Correlation Matrix as Normalized Covariance
examples.code:
# fragment: continues the previous example (needs np, X and cov_numpy)
stds = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov_numpy))
corr_manual = cov_numpy / np.outer(stds, stds)
corr_numpy = np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False)

print(np.allclose(corr_manual, corr_numpy))
print(np.round(corr_numpy, 3))
examples.explanation: `np.diag(cov_numpy)` pulls out the three variances sitting on the diagonal, and `np.sqrt` turns each into a standard deviation; `np.outer(stds, stds)` builds the 3-by-3 matrix of every pairwise product sigma_i * sigma_j, positioned where the matching covariance sits in `cov_numpy`, so the elementwise division rescales each entry by the right pair of standard deviations. The result matches `np.corrcoef`: correlation is covariance measured in standard deviations instead of the features' original units. It is also why every diagonal entry is 1.0: a feature's variance divided by its own standard deviation squared is 1.

examples.title: Zero Correlation Despite a Perfectly Deterministic Relationship
examples.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 13)
y = x ** 2

X = np.column_stack([x, y])
corr = np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False)
print(np.round(corr, 4))
print("corr(x, x^2) =", round(corr[0, 1], 4))
examples.explanation: y is computed from x with no randomness, the strongest possible dependence, yet the printed correlation is 0.0. The parabola is symmetric around x = 0 over this evenly spaced range, so the falling trend on the left half and the rising trend on the right contribute equal and opposite amounts to the correlation, and they cancel. A correlation matrix reports only *linear* co-movement; it is blind to curved or symmetric relationships however strong or deterministic they are.

misconceptions.description: A near-zero entry in a covariance or correlation matrix means those two features are statistically independent, or at least practically unrelated.
misconceptions.clarification: Covariance and correlation are computed entirely from sums of products of deviations from the mean, which makes them detectors of *linear* co-movement only. A feature and its own square (x and x^2 over a range symmetric around the mean) are deterministically related, so knowing x tells you x^2 exactly, yet their correlation is 0 because the relationship curves instead of trending in one linear direction. Independence implies zero correlation, but zero correlation does not imply independence; ruling out nonlinear structure requires other tools (scatterplots, mutual information, or letting a flexible model like a tree or neural network see the raw features directly).
misconceptions.fact: Covariance and correlation are computed entirely from sums of products of deviations from the mean, which makes them detectors of *linear* co-movement only.

misconceptions.description: A sample covariance matrix computed from real data occasionally shows a tiny negative eigenvalue, so covariance matrices aren't really always positive semi-definite in practice -- that's just a theoretical idealization.
misconceptions.clarification: A true covariance matrix is mathematically guaranteed to be positive semi-definite, with no exceptions -- v^T Sigma v equals Var(v^T X), and variance can never be negative for any real vector v. A tiny negative eigenvalue observed in code (something like -1e-16 instead of exactly 0) is floating-point round-off on what is mathematically a zero eigenvalue, not a violation of the PSD property. This happens routinely whenever the true rank of the covariance matrix is lower than its dimension, most commonly when the sample size n is smaller than the number of features p, which makes the sample covariance matrix exactly singular (rank at most n - 1) and pushes several of its eigenvalues to sit right at the noisy edge of zero.
misconceptions.fact: A true covariance matrix is mathematically guaranteed to be positive semi-definite, with no exceptions -- v^T Sigma v equals Var(v^T X), and variance can never be negative for any real vector v.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? Think about the relationship between the two columns before computing anything.
exercises.code:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([
    [1.0, 5.0],
    [2.0, 4.0],
    [3.0, 3.0],
    [4.0, 2.0],
    [5.0, 1.0],
])

print(np.cov(X, rowvar=False))
print(np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False))
hints: Look at the two columns side by side: as column 0 goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, what does column 1 do at each step?
This is a perfectly linear relationship (column 1 = 6 - column 0), just in the negative direction -- what should that mean for both the covariance and the correlation coefficient?

Compute the variance of a single column first (it's the same for both columns here by symmetry), then think about what the off-diagonal covariance and correlation must be given a perfect negative linear relationship.
exercises.expectedAnswer: np.cov prints [[2.5, -2.5], [-2.5, 2.5]] and np.corrcoef prints [[1.0, -1.0], [-1.0, 1.0]]. Both columns individually have variance 2.5 (values 1..5 and 5..1 have identical spread), and because column 1 is an exact negative linear function of column 0 (column1 = 6 - column0), the covariance between them equals the negative of that shared variance, and the correlation is exactly -1.0, the strongest possible negative linear relationship.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Each column has mean 3 and the deviations from the mean are -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 for column 0 and 2, 1, 0, -1, -2 for column 1 -- exact negatives of each other, row for row. The diagonal entries of np.cov are each column's own variance: sum of squared deviations (4+1+0+1+4=10) divided by (n-1)=4, giving 2.5 for both. The off-diagonal entry is the sum of the products of the deviations (-2*2 + -1*1 + 0*0 + 1*-1 + 2*-2 = -4-1+0-1-4 = -10) divided by 4, giving -2.5 -- the negative of the variance, exactly as expected for a perfect negative linear relationship. Dividing by the standard deviations (sqrt(2.5) each) to get the correlation matrix turns -2.5 into -2.5 / (sqrt(2.5)*sqrt(2.5)) = -2.5/2.5 = -1.0, and every diagonal entry of a correlation matrix is always exactly 1.0 by construction.

X here has 5 rows (samples) and 3 columns (features) -- does np.cov's default assumption match that layout, or the opposite one?

exercises.solutionCode:
import numpy as np

def feature_covariance(X):
    # X has shape (n_samples, n_features)
    return np.cov(X, rowvar=False)

X = np.array([
    [2.0, 1.0, 5.0],
    [3.0, 2.0, 4.0],
    [5.0, 4.0, 2.0],
    [7.0, 5.0, 1.0],
    [8.0, 6.0, 0.5],
])

cov = feature_covariance(X)
print(cov.shape)   # (3, 3), as intended
exercises.solutionExplanation: np.cov defaults to rowvar=True, meaning it assumes each row of the input is a separate variable and each column is a separate observation of all those variables -- the opposite of the standard machine-learning convention used here, where each of the 5 rows is a sample and each of the 3 columns is a feature. With the default, np.cov treated the 5 rows as 5 'variables' each observed 3 times, producing a 5x5 covariance matrix that describes relationships between samples, which is meaningless for this purpose. Passing rowvar=False tells np.cov that columns are the variables of interest, correctly producing the intended 3x3 feature-by-feature covariance matrix. This is a common numpy bug in statistics code because it raises no error: it returns a valid matrix of a different shape that describes something other than what you intended.

assessments.prompt: In a p-by-p covariance matrix Sigma computed from a feature matrix X, what do the diagonal entries Sigma[i, i] represent?
options: The variance of feature i by itself.
The number of samples used to compute the covariance matrix.
Always exactly 1, since a feature is perfectly related to itself.
The correlation of feature i with every other feature, averaged together.
assessments.explanation: The diagonal entry Sigma[i, i] is Cov(X_i, X_i), which is mathematically identical to Var(X_i) -- the covariance matrix's diagonal is just each feature's ordinary scalar variance, generalized into matrix form. The “The correlation of feature i with every…” option confuses the covariance matrix with something like an average off-diagonal summary, which isn't what the diagonal holds. The “The number of samples used to compute…” option is a property of the dataset, not something stored in the covariance matrix itself. The “Always exactly 1, since a feature…” option describes the correlation matrix's diagonal (always exactly 1 after normalization by standard deviations), not the covariance matrix's diagonal, which retains each feature's original variance in its original squared units and is generally not 1.

assessments.prompt: Why is the correlation matrix generally preferred over the raw covariance matrix for comparing the strength of relationships across different pairs of features at a glance?
options: Covariance matrices cannot be computed for more than two features at a time.
Correlation matrices are computationally cheaper to calculate than covariance matrices.
Correlation is always a larger number than covariance, making differences easier to see.

Correlation is scale-invariant -- dividing each covariance by the product of the corresponding standard deviations removes the dependence on the original measurement units, so every entry is directly comparable on a fixed [-1, 1] scale.
assessments.explanation: Covariance's magnitude depends on the units the features are measured in: income in dollars versus thousands of dollars changes the raw covariance by a factor of a thousand with no change in the strength of the relationship. Dividing by the two features' standard deviations cancels that dependence, landing every entry in a fixed, comparable [-1, 1] range. The “Correlation is always a larger number…” option is not a general truth (correlation magnitudes are bounded by 1 and are often smaller in absolute value than covariance, depending on units). The “Correlation matrices are computationally cheaper to calculate…” option is false; both are simple, comparably cheap matrix computations. The “Covariance matrices cannot be computed for more…” option is false; the covariance matrix formula generalizes cleanly to any number of features.

assessments.prompt: A correlation matrix entry between features A and B is computed as 0.02, very close to zero. Which conclusion is actually justified by that number alone?
options: A causes B, but only weakly.
A and B must be measured in incompatible units.
A and B show no consistent *linear* relationship in this data; a strong nonlinear relationship between them is still entirely possible and would not be detected by this number.
A and B are statistically independent.
assessments.explanation: Correlation is built purely from linear covariation, so a value near zero only rules out a linear relationship; the x-versus-x-squared example in the concept shows a deterministic relationship producing a 0.0 correlation, because the relationship curves. The “A and B are statistically independent” option overclaims: zero correlation is necessary but not sufficient for independence. The “A and B must be measured in incompatible units” option is unrelated: correlation is unit-free, so measurement units never affect it. The “A causes B, but only weakly” option wrongly infers causation from a correlation coefficient, which describes association only and says nothing about causal mechanism.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague who has just seen a p-by-p correlation matrix for the first time what the matrix's structure guarantees mathematically (symmetry and positive semi-definiteness), what the entries actually mean, and the single most important limitation to keep in mind when reading it.
assessments.modelAnswer: A correlation matrix -- and the covariance matrix it's built from -- is always symmetric, because the covariance between feature i and feature j is computed the same way regardless of which one you call 'first,' so Sigma[i,j] always equals Sigma[j,i]. It's also always positive semi-definite, meaning for any way you combine the features into a single linear combination, the resulting quantity's variance can never come out negative; this is forced by the matrix being built from the variances of linear combinations of the features, and variance is never negative. That guarantees every eigenvalue of the matrix is zero or positive, which is the property PCA relies on later to treat eigenvalues as amounts of variance along orthogonal directions. Each entry rho[i,j] tells you the strength and direction of the *linear* relationship between feature i and feature j, rescaled by their standard deviations so the number sits in a fixed range from -1 (perfect negative linear relationship) through 0 (no linear relationship) to +1 (perfect positive linear relationship), with the diagonal always exactly 1 because every feature is perfectly linearly related to itself. The main limitation is that it measures linear relationships only: two features can be strongly, even deterministically, related in a nonlinear or symmetric way -- a variable and its own square is the classic case -- and still show a correlation of essentially zero, so a matrix full of small numbers is evidence against linear relationships specifically, never proof that the underlying features have nothing to do with each other.

concepts.title: Mahalanobis Distance
concepts.description: Mahalanobis distance is Euclidean distance measured after accounting for a dataset's correlation and differing feature scales, so it can correctly judge a point as a severe outlier even when a plain Euclidean measurement would call it unremarkable.
learningObjectives: State the Mahalanobis distance formula and explain the role of each term, especially the inverse covariance matrix.
Explain why Mahalanobis distance is 'Euclidean distance after whitening' -- rescaling and de-correlating the data before measuring distance.
Construct a concrete example where two points sit at equal Euclidean distance from a mean but very different Mahalanobis distances, and explain why.
Compute Mahalanobis distance in numpy using the inverse covariance matrix, and cross-check the result against scipy's implementation.
Apply Mahalanobis distance to flag multivariate outliers using a chi-squared distance threshold, and explain why the covariance estimate itself must be trustworthy for this to work.

sections.heading: Why Plain Euclidean Distance Lies When Features Are Correlated
sections.body:
Ordinary Euclidean distance treats every feature axis as independent and equally scaled: sqrt(sum of squared differences). That is the wrong notion of distance whenever features are correlated or on very different scales, which describes most real feature matrices. Imagine two features that are strongly positively correlated in normal data -- say, a person's height in centimeters and their shoe size, or two sensor readings that physically tend to move together. A new data point that follows that same correlation (both values move up together) is perfectly ordinary, even if both individual values are somewhat large. A point at the *same Euclidean distance* from the mean that breaks the correlation (one value far above average while its partner is far below) is a much less plausible observation, yet a ruler can't tell the two apart.

**Mahalanobis distance** fixes this. Given a mean vector mu and covariance matrix Sigma describing the 'normal' spread and correlation structure of the data, the Mahalanobis distance of a point x is:

```
d(x, mu) = sqrt( (x - mu)^T @ Sigma_inv @ (x - mu) )
```

where `Sigma_inv` is the inverse of the covariance matrix. When Sigma happens to be the identity matrix (every feature has variance 1 and every pair has zero covariance -- i.e., independent, standardized features), this formula reduces to ordinary Euclidean distance, because Sigma_inv is the identity and the quadratic form collapses to a sum of squares. So Mahalanobis distance is Euclidean distance generalized to data whose natural axes are correlated and unequally scaled.

sections.heading: The Formula as a Whitening Transform
sections.body:
The clearest way to see the formula is as 'Euclidean distance, after first transforming the data into a coordinate system where it's uncorrelated and unit-scaled' -- a process called **whitening**. Because Sigma is symmetric and, when invertible, positive definite, it can be written as Sigma = V @ Lambda @ V^T (its eigendecomposition, covered in full in the PCA concept next), which means Sigma_inv = V @ Lambda_inv @ V^T, and there exists a matrix W (built from V and the inverse square roots of the eigenvalues in Lambda) such that Sigma_inv = W^T @ W. Substituting this into the Mahalanobis formula gives d(x, mu) = sqrt((x - mu)^T @ W^T @ W @ (x - mu)) = ||W @ (x - mu)||, the plain Euclidean norm of the *transformed* vector W @ (x - mu).

What W actually does is rotate the data onto its principal axes (the eigenvectors of Sigma) and then rescale each axis by the inverse of its standard deviation along that axis. After the transform the data has unit variance in every direction and no correlation between axes, the condition under which plain Euclidean distance is the right notion of 'how far.' Mahalanobis distance is Euclidean distance measured in standard deviations along the data's own axes instead of the raw units and orientation the features happened to be recorded in. So the same displacement from the mean can give a small Mahalanobis distance in a direction the data varies a lot in and a huge one in a direction it almost never varies in: the whitening step stretches the tight, rarely-varying directions and compresses the loose, frequently-varying ones.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Identical Euclidean Distance, Wildly Different Mahalanobis Distance
sections.body:
Consider a 2-dimensional dataset centered at the origin with a strong positive correlation of 0.9 between its two features -- covariance matrix Sigma = [[1.0, 0.9], [0.9, 1.0]]. Two candidate points, A = (2, 2) and B = (2, -2), sit at the same Euclidean distance from the origin, sqrt(2^2 + 2^2) = 2.83, since Euclidean distance ignores the data's correlation structure. But point A moves in the direction the two features are known to move together (both up), while point B moves against that grain (one up, one down), which the strong positive correlation says should almost never happen.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import mahalanobis

mu = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
Sigma = np.array([[1.0, 0.9],
                   [0.9, 1.0]])
Sigma_inv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma)

A = np.array([2.0, 2.0])    # consistent with the positive correlation
B = np.array([2.0, -2.0])   # inconsistent with the positive correlation

def mahalanobis_dist(x, mu, Sigma_inv):
    diff = x - mu
    return np.sqrt(diff @ Sigma_inv @ diff)

print("Euclidean A:", np.linalg.norm(A - mu))       # 2.828...
print("Euclidean B:", np.linalg.norm(B - mu))       # 2.828... -- identical
print("Mahalanobis A:", mahalanobis_dist(A, mu, Sigma_inv))   # 2.05
print("Mahalanobis B:", mahalanobis_dist(B, mu, Sigma_inv))   # 8.94 -- over 4x larger
print("scipy check:", mahalanobis(A, mu, Sigma_inv), mahalanobis(B, mu, Sigma_inv))
```

The two points are equally far away by ruler-distance, but B's Mahalanobis distance (8.94) is more than four times A's (2.05). A is unremarkable given this data's correlation structure; B is a severe outlier, a combination of values that should almost never co-occur, and only Mahalanobis distance sees the difference.

sections.heading: Outlier and Anomaly Detection with a Chi-Squared Threshold
sections.body:
Under the assumption that the data is (approximately) multivariate normal, the squared Mahalanobis distance of a random draw from that distribution follows a **chi-squared distribution with p degrees of freedom**, where p is the number of features -- which turns Mahalanobis distance into a principled anomaly detector instead of just a ranking. A threshold at, say, the 97.5th percentile of that chi-squared distribution flags any point whose squared Mahalanobis distance exceeds it, with a known false-positive rate: about 2.5% of truly normal points exceed it by chance.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.covariance import EmpiricalCovariance
from scipy.stats import chi2

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, p = 300, 2
true_cov = np.array([[1.0, 0.8], [0.8, 1.0]])
L = np.linalg.cholesky(true_cov)
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p)) @ L.T          # 300 normal, correlated points
outliers = np.array([[3.0, -3.0], [-4.0, 4.0], [0.0, 4.0]])
X_full = np.vstack([X, outliers])           # inject 3 clear outliers

cov_est = EmpiricalCovariance().fit(X_full)
d2 = cov_est.mahalanobis(X_full)            # squared Mahalanobis distances
threshold = chi2.ppf(0.975, df=p)
flagged = np.where(d2 > threshold)[0]

print("threshold:", round(threshold, 3))    # 7.378
print("flagged indices:", flagged)          # includes indices 300, 301, 302
print("d^2 of injected outliers:", np.round(d2[-3:], 2))   # e.g. [51.25, 90.67, 25.09], all far above threshold
```

All three injected outliers are flagged, along with four of the 300 normal points that landed far out by chance (indices 69, 113, 124 and 252 with this seed), in line with the roughly 2.5% false-positive rate. The same technique underlies many anomaly and out-of-distribution detectors: fit a mean and covariance to a model's embeddings on 'normal' training data, then flag new inputs whose Mahalanobis distance from that distribution is unusually large as likely outliers or novel classes. The mathematics is the same as for rows of a tabular dataset, applied to learned feature vectors instead of raw columns. The approach is only as good as the covariance estimate. Here the estimate was fit on `X_full`, so the injected outliers inflate it slightly; with many outliers this masks them, and robust estimators such as scikit-learn's `MinCovDet` exist for that case. A reliable full covariance matrix also needs enough samples relative to the number of features, which the misconceptions below cover.

examples.title: Same Euclidean Distance, Very Different Mahalanobis Distance
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.distance import mahalanobis

mu = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
Sigma = np.array([[1.0, 0.9],
                   [0.9, 1.0]])
Sigma_inv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma)

A = np.array([2.0, 2.0])
B = np.array([2.0, -2.0])

def mahalanobis_dist(x, mu, Sigma_inv):
    diff = x - mu
    return np.sqrt(diff @ Sigma_inv @ diff)

print("Euclidean:", np.linalg.norm(A - mu), np.linalg.norm(B - mu))
print("Mahalanobis:", mahalanobis_dist(A, mu, Sigma_inv), mahalanobis_dist(B, mu, Sigma_inv))
print("scipy check:", mahalanobis(A, mu, Sigma_inv), mahalanobis(B, mu, Sigma_inv))
examples.explanation: Both A and B sit at Euclidean distance 2.828 from the origin, so Euclidean distance cannot distinguish them. Once the strong positive correlation (0.9) between the two features is accounted for via Sigma_inv, A (which moves with the correlation, both coordinates up together) gets a Mahalanobis distance of about 2.05, unremarkable for this data, while B (which moves against the correlation, one coordinate up and the other down) gets a Mahalanobis distance of about 8.94, more than four times larger. The scipy.spatial.distance.mahalanobis function takes the two points and the *inverse* covariance matrix (its `VI` argument), not the covariance matrix itself, and matches the hand-rolled formula. Passing the covariance matrix by mistake raises no error and returns a wrong number.

examples.explanation: sklearn's `EmpiricalCovariance` fits a mean and covariance matrix to the data and has a `.mahalanobis()` method that returns the *squared* Mahalanobis distance of every row, with no manual inversion. `chi2.ppf(0.975, df=p)` looks up the 97.5th percentile of the chi-squared distribution with p=2 degrees of freedom, giving a principled cutoff (about 7.38 here) if the bulk of the data is multivariate normal; any point whose squared Mahalanobis distance clears it is flagged. All three injected outliers are caught, each well above the threshold, along with a few ordinary points that clear it by chance, the false-positive rate implied by a 97.5th-percentile cutoff.

misconceptions.description: Mahalanobis distance is just Euclidean distance multiplied by some constant scaling factor.
misconceptions.clarification: If that were true, every direction away from the mean would be stretched or compressed by the same amount, and A and B in the worked example -- both at identical Euclidean distance from the mean -- would necessarily also have identical Mahalanobis distances. They don't: A measures 2.05 and B measures 8.94, more than four times larger, despite the same Euclidean distance. Mahalanobis distance applies a direction-dependent (anisotropic) transformation derived from the covariance matrix's own eigenvectors and eigenvalues -- it stretches distance along the data's naturally tight, low-variance directions and compresses it along the data's naturally loose, high-variance and correlated directions, which a single scaling constant cannot do.

misconceptions.description: You can always safely compute Mahalanobis distance by taking whatever sample covariance matrix you calculated and calling np.linalg.inv on it.
misconceptions.clarification: A sample covariance matrix is only guaranteed to be invertible when it's full rank, which fails whenever there are fewer samples than features (n <= p, common with high-dimensional embeddings), whenever two features are exact or near-exact linear combinations of each other, or whenever a feature has (near) zero variance. In any of these cases, np.linalg.inv either raises a LinAlgError or, worse, returns numerically garbage if the matrix is only ill-conditioned rather than exactly singular. The practical fixes are to use a regularized covariance estimator (shrinkage estimators like Ledoit-Wolf, or adding a small multiple of the identity matrix before inverting), reduce dimensionality first (e.g. with PCA), or fall back to a pseudo-inverse (np.linalg.pinv) . Calling np.linalg.inv on a sample covariance matrix without checking its condition number (np.linalg.cond) risks silently wrong distances.

exercises.prompt: Given this covariance matrix describing a strong negative correlation between two features, which of point C or point D is farther from the origin in Mahalanobis distance, and roughly how do their Euclidean distances compare? Reason it through before running anything.
exercises.code:
import numpy as np

mu = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
Sigma = np.array([[1.0, -0.9],
                   [-0.9, 1.0]])
Sigma_inv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma)

C = np.array([2.0, -2.0])   # moves WITH the negative correlation
D = np.array([2.0, 2.0])    # moves AGAINST the negative correlation

def maha(x, mu, Sigma_inv):
    diff = x - mu
    return np.sqrt(diff @ Sigma_inv @ diff)

print("Euclidean:", np.linalg.norm(C - mu), np.linalg.norm(D - mu))
print("Mahalanobis:", maha(C, mu, Sigma_inv), maha(D, mu, Sigma_inv))
hints: Both C and D are the same distance from the origin by the plain Pythagorean formula -- sqrt(2^2 + 2^2) either way, regardless of the signs -- so the Euclidean line should print two identical numbers.
The correlation here is -0.9: the two features strongly tend to move in OPPOSITE directions. Which of C = (2, -2) or D = (2, 2) is consistent with that pattern, and which one contradicts it?

The point that goes against the data's natural correlation structure is the one the covariance matrix treats as unusual -- that's the one whose Mahalanobis distance should come out much larger, mirroring the A-vs-B example in the concept but with the correlation's sign flipped.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Both Euclidean distances print the same value, 2.8284271247461903, since Euclidean distance ignores the correlation structure entirely. Mahalanobis distance is much larger for D than for C: C = (2, -2) moves consistently with the -0.9 negative correlation (one feature up, the other down, exactly the pattern the data expects), so it gets a small Mahalanobis distance, while D = (2, 2) moves against that correlation (both features up together, which strong negative correlation says should rarely happen), giving it a much larger Mahalanobis distance -- numerically, Mahalanobis(C) is about 2.05 and Mahalanobis(D) is about 8.94.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This is a mirror image of the worked example in the concept with the sign of the correlation flipped: with Sigma = [[1, -0.9], [-0.9, 1]], the data expects the two features to move in opposite directions. Point C = (2, -2) does exactly that -- one coordinate up, the other down -- so it aligns with the data's natural spread and gets a small Mahalanobis distance (about 2.05). Point D = (2, 2) has both coordinates moving up together, directly contradicting the strong negative correlation, so it gets a much larger Mahalanobis distance (about 8.94) despite having the identical Euclidean distance from the origin as C. The lesson generalizes: what makes a point 'far' in the Mahalanobis sense is not how large its coordinates are in isolation, but whether the *combination* of its coordinate values is consistent with the correlation structure the covariance matrix encodes.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to compute the Mahalanobis distance of every point in X from the data's own mean, but it crashes. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([
    [1.0, 2.0, 2.0],
    [2.0, 3.0, 3.0],
    [3.0, 1.0, 1.0],
    [4.0, 5.0, 5.0],
    [5.0, 2.0, 2.0],
])   # feature 2 is an exact duplicate of feature 1

mu = X.mean(axis=0)
Sigma = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)
Sigma_inv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma)   # crashes: LinAlgError: Singular matrix

def maha(x, mu, Sigma_inv):
    diff = x - mu
    return np.sqrt(diff @ Sigma_inv @ diff)

distances = [maha(x, mu, Sigma_inv) for x in X]
print(distances)
hints: Print Sigma and look closely at its rows and columns -- are any two of them identical, or exact multiples of each other?
Column 2 of X is an exact copy of column 1, which means Sigma is rank-deficient (not full rank) -- a matrix like that has no true inverse, which is what the LinAlgError is reporting.

You don't need np.linalg.inv specifically -- either drop the redundant duplicated feature before computing Sigma, or use np.linalg.pinv (the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse), which handles singular matrices gracefully instead of raising an error.
exercises.solutionCode:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([
    [1.0, 2.0, 2.0],
    [2.0, 3.0, 3.0],
    [3.0, 1.0, 1.0],
    [4.0, 5.0, 5.0],
    [5.0, 2.0, 2.0],
])

# Fix option 1: drop the exact-duplicate feature before computing Sigma
X_dedup = X[:, [0, 1]]
mu = X_dedup.mean(axis=0)
Sigma = np.cov(X_dedup, rowvar=False)
Sigma_inv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma)   # now full rank, inverts cleanly

def maha(x, mu, Sigma_inv):
    diff = x - mu
    return np.sqrt(diff @ Sigma_inv @ diff)

distances = [maha(x, mu, Sigma_inv) for x in X_dedup]
print(distances)

# Fix option 2 (keep all 3 columns): use the pseudo-inverse instead of the true inverse
mu_full = X.mean(axis=0)
Sigma_full = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)
Sigma_pinv = np.linalg.pinv(Sigma_full)
distances_full = [maha(x, mu_full, Sigma_pinv) for x in X]
print(distances_full)
exercises.solutionExplanation: Feature 2 is an exact copy of feature 1, so the covariance matrix Sigma has two identical rows and two identical columns, making it rank-deficient (rank 2 instead of the full rank 3) and therefore singular -- it has no true matrix inverse, which is what np.linalg.inv's LinAlgError is reporting, not a bug in the surrounding logic. There are two legitimate fixes: remove the redundant duplicated feature before computing Sigma at all, which is the more principled fix, since a duplicated feature carries no additional information; or, if all three columns must be retained for some other reason, replace np.linalg.inv with np.linalg.pinv, the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse, which handles singular and near-singular matrices without raising an error by using only the well-defined part of the matrix's structure. Swapping in pinv without understanding why Sigma is singular can mask a data-quality problem, so diagnose the redundancy even when pinv is the fix you choose.

assessments.prompt: In the formula d(x, mu) = sqrt((x - mu)^T @ Sigma_inv @ (x - mu)), what specific role does Sigma_inv (the inverse covariance matrix) play?
options: It normalizes the result so every Mahalanobis distance falls strictly between 0 and 1.

It rescales and de-correlates the displacement (x - mu) so that distance is measured in a coordinate system where the data's natural spread is uniform in every direction, reducing to plain Euclidean distance exactly when Sigma is the identity matrix.
It converts the distance from a scalar into a vector so it can be compared componentwise.
It has no mathematical necessity and is included only as a convention; any positive definite matrix could be substituted with the same result.
assessments.explanation: Sigma_inv implements the whitening transform described above: it can be factored as W^T @ W, and substituting that into the formula shows the Mahalanobis distance is the plain Euclidean norm of W @ (x - mu), where W rotates onto the data's principal axes and rescales each one by its inverse standard deviation. When Sigma is the identity matrix (independent, unit-variance features), Sigma_inv is also the identity, and the formula collapses to ordinary Euclidean distance. The “It converts the distance from a scalar…” option misdescribes the formula as producing a vector rather than a scalar. The “It has no mathematical necessity…” option is false: the actual inverse covariance matrix, not an arbitrary substitute, is what makes the distance reflect this dataset's correlation and scale structure. The “It normalizes the result so every Mahalanobis…” option is false; Mahalanobis distance is unbounded above and is not restricted to [0, 1].

assessments.prompt: Two points, P and Q, are at identical Euclidean distance from a dataset's mean. P's coordinates move consistently with the data's strong positive correlation; Q's coordinates move directly against it. What should happen to their Mahalanobis distances?
options: They remain equal, since Mahalanobis distance is just a rescaled version of Euclidean distance by a single constant factor.
Q's Mahalanobis distance should be smaller, because moving against a positive correlation always reduces distance.
Mahalanobis distance cannot be computed at all when the two features are correlated.
P's Mahalanobis distance should be noticeably smaller than Q's.
assessments.explanation: This mirrors the A-versus-B example above: a point consistent with the data's correlation structure (both features moving together, matching a positive correlation) is not unusual and gets a small Mahalanobis distance, while a point that contradicts that structure (features moving in opposite directions despite a strong positive correlation) is unusual and gets a much larger one, even at identical Euclidean distance. The “They remain equal, since Mahalanobis distance…” option is the misconception refuted above: the rescaling is direction-dependent, not a single constant. The “Q's Mahalanobis distance should be smaller…” option has the direction of the effect backwards. The “Mahalanobis distance cannot be computed at all…” option is false; Mahalanobis distance is designed for correlated features, and its covariance input is what carries the correlation.

assessments.prompt: Under the assumption that data is approximately multivariate normal, the squared Mahalanobis distance of a random draw follows what distribution, and how is that fact used for outlier detection?
options: It depends entirely on the specific dataset and has no general distributional form that can be used for thresholding.

A chi-squared distribution with p degrees of freedom (p = number of features); a high percentile of that distribution (e.g. the 97.5th) is used as a threshold, and points whose squared Mahalanobis distance exceeds it are flagged, with a known approximate false-positive rate.
A uniform distribution between 0 and 1, so any distance above 0.95 is flagged.
A standard normal distribution; points beyond 1.96 are flagged as outliers, exactly as with a single scalar feature.
assessments.explanation: Squared Mahalanobis distance under multivariate normality follows a chi-squared distribution with p degrees of freedom, so scipy.stats.chi2.ppf(0.975, df=p) gives a principled threshold with a known false-positive rate of about 2.5%, rather than an arbitrary cutoff. The “A standard normal distribution; points beyond 1.96…” option wrongly imports the scalar z-score rule, which doesn't generalize correctly to multiple correlated dimensions. The “A uniform distribution between 0 and 1…” option invents an unrelated uniform-distribution rule. The “It depends entirely on the specific dataset…” option is incorrect -- the chi-squared result holds for any multivariate normal, whatever the dataset's values, which is what makes it a general-purpose threshold.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague why Mahalanobis distance is a better tool than plain Euclidean distance for detecting outliers or anomalies in correlated, multi-feature data, and what has to go right (about the covariance estimate) for that advantage to actually hold up in practice.
assessments.modelAnswer: Plain Euclidean distance treats every feature axis as independent and identically scaled, so it can only ever measure how far a point's raw coordinates are from the mean's raw coordinates, with no notion of whether that particular combination of values is actually plausible given how the features normally relate to each other. Mahalanobis distance fixes this by folding the inverse covariance matrix into the distance calculation, which amounts to first rotating and rescaling the data onto its own natural, uncorrelated axes -- a whitening transform -- and only then measuring plain distance in that corrected coordinate system. The practical payoff is that two points can sit at identical Euclidean distance from the mean while having very different Mahalanobis distances: a point whose feature combination is consistent with the data's real correlation structure gets treated as unremarkable, while a point whose combination contradicts that structure -- for example, breaking a strong positive correlation by having one feature far above average and its usual partner far below average -- gets correctly flagged as unusual, something Euclidean distance is structurally blind to. This is the mechanism behind many practical anomaly and out-of-distribution detection methods: fit a mean and covariance to a model's normal feature representations, then flag new points whose Mahalanobis distance from that fitted distribution clears a chi-squared-derived threshold. For this to work, though, the covariance matrix itself has to be a trustworthy estimate of the real relationships in the data -- with too few samples relative to the number of features, or with exactly or nearly duplicated features, the sample covariance matrix becomes singular or ill-conditioned, and either its inverse doesn't exist or, worse, exists but is numerically garbage, producing Mahalanobis distances that reflect estimation noise rather than genuine outlyingness. Regularized covariance estimators, dimensionality reduction beforehand, or simply collecting more samples relative to the feature count are the standard remedies.

concepts.title: PCA via Eigendecomposition and Singular Value Decomposition
concepts.description: Principal Component Analysis finds the orthogonal directions of maximum variance in a dataset by eigendecomposing its covariance matrix -- or, equivalently and more numerically stably, by taking the singular value decomposition of the centered data matrix directly -- making it the standard technique for reducing embedding and feature dimensionality in ML pipelines.
learningObjectives: State PCA's objective precisely: find orthogonal directions, ranked by variance explained, that a dataset's projections onto them maximize.
Derive principal components as the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, and principal values as the corresponding eigenvalues.
Explain the equivalent SVD-based formulation of PCA and why it is more numerically stable than eigendecomposing the covariance matrix directly.
Compute the explained variance ratio for each component and use it to decide how many components to keep.
Apply sklearn.decomposition.PCA to reduce a feature or embedding matrix's dimensionality and interpret the transformed output.
Explain why centering (and often scaling) the data before PCA is required, and what happens to the result when it's skipped.

sections.heading: PCA's Goal: Orthogonal Directions of Maximum Variance
sections.body:
**Principal Component Analysis (PCA)** answers a geometric question with no labels involved: of all the directions you could project the data onto, which preserves the most variance (spread)? That direction is the **first principal component**. Having found it, PCA asks the same question again, but restricted to directions orthogonal (perpendicular) to the first component: which of those remaining directions captures the most of whatever variance is left? That's the second principal component. This repeats until you have as many orthogonal directions as the data has dimensions, each one capturing the most variance possible given everything already claimed by the components before it.

Maximizing variance is a sensible objective because variance is a proxy for how much a direction tells you about how the points differ from each other. Along a direction the data barely varies, nearly every point projects to nearly the same value, so it says almost nothing about which point is which; a high-variance direction separates points well. Keeping the top principal components keeps the directions that separate points most and drops those that separate them least, without ever looking at a label. Variance is only a proxy, though: a low-variance direction can still be the one that matters for a particular task.

sections.heading: The Eigendecomposition Formulation: Principal Components as Eigenvectors of Sigma
sections.body:
The directions that maximize variance are the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix Sigma, and the variance captured along each is the corresponding eigenvalue. This is a provable result, not a heuristic. Because Sigma is always symmetric and positive semi-definite (established in the previous concept), it admits an eigendecomposition Sigma = V @ Lambda @ V^T where V's columns are orthonormal eigenvectors and Lambda is a diagonal matrix of nonnegative eigenvalues. Sorting the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs from largest eigenvalue to smallest gives the principal components in order: the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue is the first principal component, the eigenvector with the second-largest eigenvalue is the second principal component, and so on. Projecting the centered data onto the top k eigenvectors -- computing X_centered @ V_k, where V_k holds only the first k columns of V -- is the dimensionality reduction step.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 200
z = rng.normal(size=n)                              # a shared latent signal
x1 = z + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=n)
x2 = z + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=n)
x3 = rng.normal(scale=0.05, size=n)                  # nearly independent, low-variance
X = np.column_stack([x1, x2, x3])

X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
cov = (X_centered.T @ X_centered) / (n - 1)

eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)               # ascending order by default
order = np.argsort(eigvals)[::-1]                    # re-sort descending
eigvals_sorted = eigvals[order]
eigvecs_sorted = eigvecs[:, order]

print(np.round(eigvals_sorted, 4))                   # [1.8611 0.0988 0.0029]
print(np.round(eigvals_sorted / eigvals_sorted.sum(), 4))   # [0.9482 0.0503 0.0015]
```

`np.linalg.eigh` (for symmetric/Hermitian matrices, which Sigma always is) returns eigenvalues in ascending order, so they must be reversed to get the usual 'most variance first' order; forgetting this mislabels components without any error. The three eigenvalues (1.86, 0.099, 0.003) reflect how the data was built: x1 and x2 share a strong latent signal z, so the first component captures it and accounts for 94.8% of total variance, while x3 is nearly independent low-variance noise and ends up almost entirely in the smallest component.

sections.heading: The SVD Formulation and Why It's More Numerically Stable
sections.body:
There is a second, equivalent route to the same principal components, and it is the one most implementations use, including scikit-learn's `PCA` for most inputs: the **singular value decomposition** of the centered data matrix itself, X_centered = U @ S @ V^T, where U and V have orthonormal columns and S is diagonal with nonnegative singular values. A short substitution shows the connection directly: Sigma = (X_centered^T @ X_centered) / (n - 1) = (V @ S @ U^T @ U @ S @ V^T) / (n - 1) = V @ (S^2 / (n - 1)) @ V^T, using U^T @ U = I. Comparing this to the eigendecomposition Sigma = V @ Lambda @ V^T shows that the SVD's right singular vectors V are the covariance matrix's eigenvectors, and the eigenvalues are S^2 / (n - 1), the squared singular values rescaled.

Given that the two routes are mathematically identical, why prefer computing an SVD of X_centered directly over eigendecomposing Sigma? Because forming Sigma at all squares the data matrix's **condition number** -- a measure of how numerically sensitive a matrix's computations are to small floating-point errors -- and squaring an already-large condition number can push the smallest, most delicate directions of variance below what floating-point arithmetic can represent. This is easy to demonstrate:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p = 100, 4
U, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(n, p)))
Vt, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(p, p)))
true_singular_values = np.array([1e4, 10.0, 1.0, 1e-4])   # condition number of X: 1e8
X = U @ np.diag(true_singular_values) @ Vt.T
X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)

# Route 1: form the covariance matrix, then eigendecompose (condition number of Sigma: 1e16)
cov = (X_centered.T @ X_centered) / (n - 1)
eigvals_sorted = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(cov))[::-1]
recovered_via_cov = np.sqrt(np.clip(eigvals_sorted, 0, None) * (n - 1))

# Route 2: SVD directly on the centered data matrix
_, S, _ = np.linalg.svd(X_centered, full_matrices=False)

print(recovered_via_cov)   # [9.99e+03  9.997e+00  9.889e-01  0.0]        -- smallest singular value LOST
print(np.sort(S)[::-1])    # [9.99e+03  9.997e+00  9.889e-01  9.973e-05]   -- correctly recovered
```

Here the data matrix has condition number 10^8 (plausible for badly scaled real features). Forming the covariance matrix squares that to 10^16, the limit of 64-bit floating-point precision, and the smallest singular value, 1e-4, is lost: it comes back as 0.0 through the covariance route. The SVD of the centered data never forms Sigma and recovers it (about 9.97e-05, slightly below 1e-4 because centering changes the matrix). That is why the SVD-based solvers in `sklearn.decomposition.PCA` work on the centered data matrix instead of forming a covariance matrix. Be aware that scikit-learn's default `svd_solver='auto'` can instead choose `covariance_eigh` when there are fewer than 1000 features and more than 10 times as many samples; that solver does form the covariance matrix, which is fine for well-scaled data but is exposed to the precision loss shown here.

sections.heading: Explained Variance Ratio, Choosing k, and Real ML Usage
sections.body:
The **explained variance ratio** of the i-th principal component is its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues -- the fraction of the dataset's total variance that component alone accounts for. Plotting the cumulative sum of explained variance ratios against the number of components kept, and looking for the point where adding further components stops meaningfully increasing that cumulative total (the 'elbow'), is the usual practical way to decide how many components k to retain: keep enough to capture some target fraction of total variance (90%, 95%, and 99% are common conventional thresholds), and discard the rest.

```python
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=3)
pca.fit(X)   # X from the earlier example: shared-signal x1, x2, and near-independent x3
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)          # [0.9482 0.0503 0.0015]
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.cumsum())  # [0.9482 0.9985 1.0   ]
```

Keeping only the first component retains 94.8% of total variance, a 3-to-1 reduction that loses little of what varies, because it captures the latent structure shared by x1 and x2. This is a common use of PCA in ML pipelines: shrinking a high-dimensional embedding (hundreds or thousands of dimensions from a pretrained model) to far fewer components before storage, indexing, or a downstream model, trading a small, measurable amount of variance for large savings in compute and storage. It can also denoise, since low-variance components often carry more noise than signal, though not always.

A common way to get misleading results is skipping preprocessing. PCA maximizes *variance*, which depends on scale, so a feature measured in units that produce large numbers dominates the first component regardless of how informative it is (the debugging exercise below shows this). `sklearn.decomposition.PCA` centers the data internally but does **not** scale it, so features on very different scales usually need `sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` first. PCA's objective also ignores any label: it knows nothing about what you want to predict, in contrast to LDA in the next concept, which uses class labels.

examples.title: PCA via Eigendecomposition, Cross-Checked Against sklearn
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 200
z = rng.normal(size=n)
x1 = z + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=n)
x2 = z + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=n)
x3 = rng.normal(scale=0.05, size=n)
X = np.column_stack([x1, x2, x3])

X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
cov = (X_centered.T @ X_centered) / (n - 1)
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)
order = np.argsort(eigvals)[::-1]
eigvals_sorted, eigvecs_sorted = eigvals[order], eigvecs[:, order]

pca = PCA(n_components=3).fit(X)

print(np.round(eigvals_sorted, 4))
print(np.round(pca.explained_variance_, 4))
print(abs(np.dot(eigvecs_sorted[:, 0], pca.components_[0])))   # ~1.0, same direction up to sign
examples.explanation: The manual eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix and sklearn's `PCA` produce the same eigenvalues (1.8611, 0.0988, 0.0029, matching `explained_variance_`) and the same principal directions up to a sign flip: v and -v span the same axis with the same variance, so `PCA` and a manual eigendecomposition may report opposite signs, which is why the comparison uses `abs()` on the dot product instead of checking for equal vectors. Doing this cross-check once by hand is a good way to confirm that a library call and the math it claims to implement agree.

examples.title: Numerical Precision Loss From Forming the Covariance Matrix
examples.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p = 100, 4
U, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(n, p)))
Vt, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(p, p)))
true_singular_values = np.array([1e4, 10.0, 1.0, 1e-4])
X = U @ np.diag(true_singular_values) @ Vt.T
X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)

cov = (X_centered.T @ X_centered) / (n - 1)
recovered_via_cov = np.sqrt(np.clip(np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(cov))[::-1], 0, None) * (n - 1))

_, S, _ = np.linalg.svd(X_centered, full_matrices=False)

print(recovered_via_cov)
print(np.sort(S)[::-1])
examples.explanation: The singular values span 10000 down to 0.0001 (condition number 10^8) so that the numerical failure is visible and reproducible. Forming Sigma squares the condition number to 10^16, the limit of 64-bit precision, and the smallest singular value is lost to rounding, coming back as 0.0 through the covariance route. The direct SVD never forms Sigma, so it recovers all four singular values; the smallest comes back as about 9.97e-05 rather than exactly 1e-4 because centering alters the matrix slightly. The contrast shows why numerically careful PCA implementations use an SVD of the data matrix.

examples.title: Explained Variance Ratio and Choosing How Many Components to Keep
examples.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import numpy as np

# fragment: X comes from the shared-latent-signal example above (x1, x2 share signal z; x3 is near-independent noise)
pca = PCA(n_components=3)
pca.fit(X)

print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.cumsum())

# keep enough components to retain at least 95% of total variance
k = int(np.searchsorted(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.cumsum(), 0.95) + 1)
print("components needed for >=95% variance:", k)
examples.explanation: `explained_variance_ratio_` reports [0.9482, 0.0503, 0.0015] : the first component alone accounts for 94.82% of total variance, and the cumulative sum crosses the common 95% threshold only once the second component is added (98.85%). `np.searchsorted` finds the first index in the cumulative array that is at least 0.95, and adding 1 turns that zero-based index into a component count. This picks k reproducibly instead of by eyeballing a plot, which helps when the decision has to be made automatically inside a pipeline.

misconceptions.description: PCA finds the features that are most important or most predictive for whatever downstream task (classification, regression) you ultimately care about.
misconceptions.clarification: PCA is entirely unsupervised -- it never looks at a label, and its only objective is maximizing captured variance in the input features themselves. A direction of high variance can be completely irrelevant to a label, and, more subtly, a direction of very low variance can be exactly the one direction that separates two classes perfectly; PCA cannot know this, because that would require using the label, which it never does. When predictive power for a specific label matters, a supervised dimensionality-reduction technique like LDA (the subject of the next concept) is the appropriate tool, because it uses the class labels in its objective.
misconceptions.fact: PCA is entirely unsupervised -- it never looks at a label, and its only objective is maximizing captured variance in the input features themselves.

misconceptions.description: Since PCA is defined as the eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix, that's how you should actually compute it in code -- forming Sigma and calling an eigenvalue routine on it.
misconceptions.clarification: The eigendecomposition-of-Sigma formulation and the SVD-of-the-data-matrix formulation are mathematically equivalent and produce identical principal components and variances in exact arithmetic, but they are not equally safe in floating-point arithmetic. Explicitly forming the covariance matrix squares the data's condition number, which can push small but real singular values below the precision floor of 64-bit floats and lose them. The demonstration above uses a matrix whose smallest true singular value comes back as 0.0 through the covariance route but is recovered through a direct SVD of the centered data. This is why the SVD-based solvers in `sklearn.decomposition.PCA` work on the centered data matrix instead of forming a covariance matrix.
misconceptions.fact: The eigendecomposition-of-Sigma formulation and the SVD-of-the-data-matrix formulation are mathematically equivalent and produce identical principal components and variances in exact arithmetic, but they are not equally safe in floating-point arithmetic.

exercises.prompt: This data matrix has an exact linear relationship between its two columns. What will pca.explained_variance_ratio_ print, and why?
exercises.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

X = np.array([
    [1.0, 2.0],
    [2.0, 4.0],
    [3.0, 6.0],
    [4.0, 8.0],
])

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
pca.fit(X)
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
hints: Look closely at the relationship between column 0 and column 1 -- is the second column derived from the first in some simple, exact way?
If every data point lies exactly on a single straight line through the mean, how many genuinely independent directions of variance can there possibly be, out of the 2 total dimensions?

The line here isn't horizontal or vertical, so both original columns individually have nonzero variance -- but PCA rotates to find the *best* single direction, which for perfectly collinear data captures all of it, leaving nothing for the second component.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints [1. 0.]. Every row satisfies column1 = 2 * column0 exactly, so all four points lie perfectly on a single straight line -- there is only one true direction of variation in the data, no matter how it's rotated. PCA's first component aligns with that line and captures 100% of the variance; the second component, forced to be orthogonal to the first, captures none, since there is nothing left to explain once the line itself is accounted for.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Because column 1 is exactly twice column 0 for every row, the four points (1,2), (2,4), (3,6), (4,8) are perfectly collinear -- they lie exactly on the line y = 2x, which passes through their shared mean. PCA's first principal component rotates to align with that line directly, and projecting the data onto it captures every bit of the spread in the original two columns, since there was never any variation off that line to begin with. The second principal component is constrained to be orthogonal to the first, and since the data has zero spread in every direction other than along the line, it captures exactly 0% of the variance -- hence explained_variance_ratio_ prints [1., 0.]. This is the most extreme possible case of what PCA does more gently with real, noisy, merely-correlated (rather than perfectly collinear) data: it concentrates variance into as few components as the data's effective dimensionality allows.

exercises.prompt: This code tries to use PCA to reduce two features, age (in years) and income (in dollars), down to their most informative single dimension, but the first component ends up dominated almost entirely by income, which the analyst didn't intend. Find the bug and fix it.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 500
age = rng.normal(40, 12, size=n)
