hints: PCA maximizes variance, and variance is measured in each feature's own original units -- what are the rough numeric scales of 'age in years' versus 'income in dollars' here?

Income's raw numeric values (tens of thousands) have a vastly larger variance than age's raw numeric values (tens), purely because of the units they're measured in, not because income is inherently more 'important' or more variable in any relative sense.

Standardizing both features to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler) before fitting PCA puts them on a comparable footing, so the first component can reflect genuine shared structure between them instead of just whichever feature happens to have larger raw numbers.
exercises.solutionCode:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 500
age = rng.normal(40, 12, size=n)
income = rng.normal(60000, 20000, size=n) + (age - 40) * 500

X = np.column_stack([age, income])
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)   # mean 0, std 1 for both features

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
pca.fit(X_scaled)
print(pca.components_)                 # now roughly [0.707, 0.707] -- a genuine blend of both features
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)   # e.g. [0.638, 0.362] -- reflects real shared structure, not raw units
exercises.solutionExplanation: Age has a standard deviation on the order of 12 (years), while income has a standard deviation on the order of 20000 (dollars) -- a difference of roughly three orders of magnitude that reflects the choice of measurement units, not which feature is more informative. PCA maximizes variance in whatever units it's handed, so without scaling it effectively sees only income, giving a first component that is almost entirely income (something like [0.0002, 1.0]) and reporting essentially 100% of variance explained by a feature that is just numerically larger, not more informative. Standardizing both features with StandardScaler first (subtracting each feature's mean and dividing by its own standard deviation) removes this artifact, and the resulting first component becomes a genuine, roughly even blend of both standardized features (about [0.707, 0.707]), with an explained variance ratio (about 64%/36%) that reflects real shared structure between age and income rather than an accident of units. Scale before PCA whenever features are measured in different units or very different numeric ranges.

assessments.prompt: What is the precise mathematical relationship between PCA's principal components and the covariance matrix Sigma of the (centered) data?
options: There is no precise relationship; PCA and covariance matrices are computed by unrelated procedures that happen to be used together by convention, and the components depend only on the means.
The principal components are the rows of Sigma itself, in their original order.
The principal components are the eigenvectors of Sigma, ordered by decreasing eigenvalue, with each eigenvalue equal to the variance captured along its corresponding component.
The principal components are the diagonal entries of Sigma, treated as a ranked list.
assessments.explanation: Because Sigma is symmetric positive semi-definite, it has an eigendecomposition Sigma = V @ Lambda @ V^T, and the columns of V sorted by decreasing eigenvalue in Lambda are exactly the principal components, with each eigenvalue equal to the variance of the data projected onto that direction. The “The principal components are the rows…” option confuses a matrix with its own rows, which are not directions of variance in any meaningful sense. The “The principal components are the diagonal entries…” option mistakes the diagonal (individual feature variances, ignoring all covariance structure) for the eigen-based principal directions, which generally point in entirely different directions once features are correlated. The “There is no precise relationship; PCA…” option is false: the relationship is exact and provable, not a convention.

assessments.prompt: Why do scikit-learn's SVD-based PCA solvers compute a singular value decomposition of the centered data matrix directly, rather than explicitly forming the covariance matrix and eigendecomposing it, even though both routes are mathematically equivalent?
options: Explicitly forming the covariance matrix squares the data matrix's condition number.
Forming the covariance matrix is against scikit-learn's coding style guidelines, for readability reasons unrelated to correctness.
The SVD route is dramatically faster in every case, while the covariance-eigendecomposition route always produces identical results with no downside besides speed.
Covariance matrices cannot be eigendecomposed at all using standard numerical linear algebra routines.
assessments.explanation: The numerical demonstration above shows this: with a data matrix of condition number 10^8, forming Sigma squares that to 10^16, at the edge of 64-bit floating-point precision, and the smallest true singular value (1e-4) is lost entirely (recovered as exactly 0.0) through the covariance-and-eigendecomposition route, while a direct SVD of the centered data matrix recovers it correctly. The “Forming the covariance matrix is against scikit-learn's…” option invents a stylistic rather than numerical justification. The “Covariance matrices cannot be eigendecomposed at all…” option is false; covariance matrices are routinely and successfully eigendecomposed (np.linalg.eigh does exactly this), just with the precision caveat described. The “The SVD route is dramatically faster…” option overclaims a universal speed advantage and wrongly claims the two routes always produce identical results, contradicting the numerical demonstration above of when they diverge.

assessments.prompt: A colleague standardizes nothing, fits PCA on raw features with very different numeric scales (e.g. age in years alongside income in dollars), and reports that the first principal component explains 99.9% of the variance, concluding the dataset is 'almost perfectly one-dimensional.' What is the most likely explanation?
options: PCA cannot be run on features measured in different units at all, so the reported result must be a software error.
A 99.9% explained variance ratio is mathematically impossible for any two-feature dataset.

The first component is likely dominated by whichever feature happens to have the largest raw numeric variance purely due to its units (e.g. dollars versus years), not because the dataset is genuinely close to one-dimensional in any meaningful sense.
The conclusion is almost certainly correct as stated -- PCA's explained variance ratio is scale-invariant, so this result reflects genuine underlying structure regardless of units.
assessments.explanation: The debugging exercise above shows this failure mode: age (variance on the order of hundreds, in years-squared units) and income (variance on the order of hundreds of millions, in dollars-squared units) fed into PCA without scaling produce a first component that is almost entirely income, purely because PCA maximizes variance in whatever units it's handed and income's units happen to produce much larger raw numbers. The “The conclusion is almost certainly correct…” option wrongly claims scale-invariance, which is precisely the property PCA lacks without standardization. The “PCA cannot be run on features measured…” option overstates the issue; PCA runs without error on mixed-unit data, it just produces a misleading result. The “A 99.9% explained variance ratio is mathematically…” option is false; explained variance ratios anywhere in [0, 1] are mathematically valid outcomes, including values very close to 1.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague how PCA is used to reduce the dimensionality of a high-dimensional embedding matrix in a real ML pipeline, what is gained, what is genuinely lost, and how explained variance ratio quantifies that trade-off.
assessments.modelAnswer: PCA reduces dimensionality by finding the orthogonal directions in an embedding matrix that capture the most variance, ranking them from most to least informative in that specific sense, and then projecting every embedding onto only the top k of those directions instead of keeping all of the original dimensions. Concretely, you fit PCA on a matrix of embeddings (say, 768-dimensional vectors from a pretrained model), look at explained_variance_ratio_ and its cumulative sum, and pick the smallest k whose cumulative ratio clears whatever threshold you're comfortable with -- 95% or 99% are common choices -- then transform every embedding down to just those k coordinates. What's gained is substantial: storage shrinks roughly in proportion to the dimensionality reduction, downstream computations (similarity search, clustering, feeding into another model) get faster, and, often as a genuine side benefit, the result is denoised, since directions with very little variance frequently correspond more to noise or idiosyncratic quirks than to meaningful signal. What is lost is the variance not captured by the retained components -- if you keep components explaining 95% of variance, you are discarding real information living in the remaining 5%, and that 5% is not guaranteed to be unimportant for every downstream purpose, especially if that purpose is a specific classification task PCA was never told about, since PCA's variance-maximizing objective is entirely unsupervised and blind to any label. Explained variance ratio makes the trade-off quantifiable: it reports, per component and cumulatively, what fraction of the original variance survives the reduction, turning 'how much am I giving up by compressing to k dimensions' into a number you can inspect before committing to a value of k in a production pipeline.

concepts.title: Linear and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis
concepts.description: LDA and QDA are generative classifiers that model each class's features as a multivariate Normal distribution and classify via Bayes' rule; LDA forces a shared covariance matrix across classes and gets a linear, lower-variance boundary out of it, while QDA allows a separate covariance per class and gets a more flexible but higher-variance quadratic boundary, and LDA doubles as a supervised dimensionality-reduction technique in its own right.
learningObjectives: Describe LDA and QDA as generative classifiers that model each class's feature distribution as multivariate Normal and classify new points via Bayes' rule.
Derive why a shared covariance matrix across classes (LDA's assumption) produces a linear decision boundary, while per-class covariance matrices (QDA) produce a quadratic one.
Explain the bias-variance tradeoff between LDA and QDA in terms of parameter count and required data per class.
Fit LDA and QDA with sklearn.discriminant_analysis and compare their behavior as training set size changes.
Use LDA as a supervised dimensionality-reduction technique and contrast its objective directly with PCA's unsupervised objective.

sections.heading: Generative Classification: Model the Data Within Each Class, Then Invert With Bayes' Rule
sections.body:
Most classifiers you encounter first (logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees) are **discriminative**: they directly model P(class | features) without ever describing what the features themselves look like within each class. LDA and QDA take the opposite, **generative** route: they model P(features | class), what the feature distribution looks like *for examples in class k*, and then use Bayes' rule to flip that around into the P(class | features) needed to actually classify a new point: P(Y=k | X=x) is proportional to P(X=x | Y=k) * P(Y=k), the class-conditional likelihood times the class's prior probability.

Both LDA and QDA make the same specific modeling choice for that class-conditional likelihood: assume X, given Y=k, follows a **multivariate Normal distribution** with class-specific mean vector mu_k and some covariance structure. This is a checkable assumption about the data, not a formality. It makes the decision boundary a closed-form linear or quadratic function with no iterative optimizer, and it is why LDA and QDA behave and fail differently from discriminative classifiers like logistic regression, which assume nothing about the feature distribution and model only the boundary between classes.

sections.heading: LDA: One Shared Covariance Matrix Across Every Class Produces a Linear Boundary
sections.body:
LDA's defining assumption is that every class shares the same covariance matrix Sigma -- only the class means mu_k differ, not the shape or orientation of each class's spread. Writing out the log of the ratio of two classes' posterior probabilities (the log-odds between class k and class l) and substituting in the multivariate Normal density for each, the quadratic terms in x -- the x^T @ Sigma_k^-1 @ x pieces -- are *identical* for every class because Sigma is shared, so they cancel when you take the difference between two classes' log-densities. What survives is a function that is linear in x: the decision boundary between any two classes -- the set of points where the two classes' posteriors are exactly tied -- is a straight line in 2D, a flat plane in 3D, or more generally a hyperplane in however many dimensions the features have.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
mean0, mean1 = np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.array([2.0, 2.0])
shared_cov = np.array([[1.0, 0.3], [0.3, 1.0]])   # SAME covariance for both classes

X0 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, shared_cov, size=150)
X1 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, shared_cov, size=150)
X = np.vstack([X0, X1])
y = np.array([0]*150 + [1]*150)

lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X, y)
print(lda.coef_, lda.intercept_)   # a single linear equation defines the whole boundary
```

Because LDA estimates only one covariance matrix, shared across all classes, it needs to estimate a total of p*(p+1)/2 covariance parameters regardless of how many classes there are -- a fixed cost that doesn't grow with the number of classes, and can be pooled from every training example across every class at once, which makes for a comparatively stable, low-variance estimate even when any single class has relatively few examples.

sections.heading: QDA: A Separate Covariance Per Class Produces a Quadratic Boundary, at a Cost
sections.body:
QDA relaxes the assumption LDA depends on: instead of one shared Sigma, QDA estimates a separate covariance matrix Sigma_k for every class. This means the quadratic x^T @ Sigma_k^-1 @ x terms in the log-posterior-ratio derivation no longer cancel between classes, because they now differ from class to class -- what survives in the decision boundary is a function that is quadratic in x, so the boundary between two classes can be an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola, depending on how the two classes' covariance structures actually differ, rather than being forced into a flat hyperplane the way LDA's boundary always is.

This added flexibility is not free. QDA has to estimate p*(p+1)/2 covariance parameters *separately for every class*, rather than once, pooled across all of them -- so with K classes, QDA's total covariance parameter count grows K-fold relative to LDA's, using only that one class's own examples to estimate each separate Sigma_k. This is a textbook bias-variance tradeoff: if the classes truly do have different covariance structures, QDA is less biased (its assumption matches reality better, and with enough data it will out-predict LDA), but it is also higher-variance, since each per-class covariance estimate has access to less data (only that one class's examples) and more parameters to estimate from it, making the estimate itself noisier and the resulting boundary more prone to overfitting when any individual class is short on examples.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis, QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
mean0, mean1 = np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.array([2.0, 2.0])
cov0 = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
cov1 = np.array([[3.0, 1.5], [1.5, 3.0]])   # genuinely DIFFERENT covariance from class 0

n_eval = 20000
X_eval = np.vstack([
    rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, cov0, size=n_eval),
    rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, cov1, size=n_eval),
])
y_eval = np.array([0]*n_eval + [1]*n_eval)

n_reps = 30   # average over many training sets: one small sample is too noisy
for n_per_class in [10, 20, 50, 200, 2000]:
    lda_accs, qda_accs = [], []
    for _ in range(n_reps):
        X_train = np.vstack([
            rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, cov0, size=n_per_class),
            rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, cov1, size=n_per_class),
        ])
        y_train = np.array([0]*n_per_class + [1]*n_per_class)
        lda_accs.append(LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_eval, y_eval))
        qda_accs.append(QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_eval, y_eval))
    print(n_per_class, round(np.mean(lda_accs), 4), round(np.mean(qda_accs), 4))

# 10:   LDA 0.8015  QDA 0.7898  <- LDA wins: too little data for QDA's extra parameters
# 20:   LDA 0.8194  QDA 0.8087  <- LDA still wins
# 50:   LDA 0.8293  QDA 0.8303  <- about even, QDA starts to pull ahead
# 200:  LDA 0.8325  QDA 0.8351  <- QDA's advantage grows
# 2000: LDA 0.8336  QDA 0.8366  <- QDA settles ahead, approaching the Bayes-optimal boundary
```

The true model has different covariances per class, so QDA is correctly specified and wins as training data grows. With only 10 or 20 examples per class, though, LDA's more constrained, lower-variance estimate generalizes better, because QDA cannot yet estimate its extra covariance parameters reliably. The more flexible model needs more data to earn back its flexibility: that is the bias-variance tradeoff in measured form. Each accuracy is averaged over 30 training sets because a single small training set is too noisy to show the pattern (with one draw per size and this seed, QDA happens to win at 10 per class).

sections.heading: LDA's Second Job: Supervised Dimensionality Reduction
sections.body:
LDA is not only a classifier; it is also a dimensionality-reduction technique, and a direct contrast to PCA from the previous concept. PCA finds directions that maximize *total* variance in the data, with no reference to any label at all. LDA's dimensionality-reduction objective (sometimes stated via **Fisher's criterion**) instead finds directions that maximize the ratio of *between-class* variance to *within-class* variance -- directions where the different classes' means are pulled as far apart as possible relative to how spread out each individual class is around its own mean. This produces at most (number of classes - 1) useful discriminant directions, since that's the dimensionality of the space spanned by the class means once you've subtracted off the overall mean.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

iris = load_iris()
X, y = iris.data, iris.target   # 4 features, 3 classes

X_lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2).fit_transform(X, y)   # USES y
X_pca = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)                             # ignores y entirely

for name, Z in [("LDA", X_lda), ("PCA", X_pca)]:
    means = np.array([Z[y == c].mean(axis=0) for c in np.unique(y)])
    within = np.mean([Z[y == c].std(axis=0).mean() for c in np.unique(y)])
    between = np.std(means, axis=0).mean()
    print(name, "between/within separation ratio:", round(between / within, 3))

# LDA between/within separation ratio: 3.128
# PCA between/within separation ratio: 2.253
```

Both methods reduce the 4-dimensional iris data to 2 dimensions, but LDA's projection has a clearly better between-class to within-class separation ratio (3.128 versus 2.253; this ratio is a rough metric defined in the code, not a standard statistic). LDA optimizes class separation using the labels, while PCA never considers them and chases raw variance, some of which has nothing to do with distinguishing the classes. LDA's `.fit_transform(X, y)` needs `y` for this reason. PCA's `.fit_transform(X)` has a `y=None` parameter only for pipeline compatibility and ignores it.

X = np.vstack([X0, X1])
y = np.array([0]*150 + [1]*150)

lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X, y)
print("decision function is linear: coef_ =", lda.coef_, "intercept_ =", lda.intercept_)
print("accuracy:", lda.score(X, y))
examples.explanation: Both classes were generated with the exact same covariance matrix and only different means, matching LDA's core assumption exactly, so LDA's boundary, determined entirely by the linear equation `coef_ @ x + intercept_ = 0`, separates them well. `lda.coef_` and `lda.intercept_` are the only numbers needed to describe the entire decision boundary, regardless of how many training points were used to estimate them, which is the 'decision boundary is a hyperplane' result from the derivation: once fit, a fixed-size linear equation is the whole model.

examples.title: The LDA/QDA Bias-Variance Tradeoff as Training Set Size Grows
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis, QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
mean0, mean1 = np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.array([2.0, 2.0])
cov0 = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
cov1 = np.array([[3.0, 1.5], [1.5, 3.0]])

n_eval = 20000
X_eval = np.vstack([rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, cov0, size=n_eval),
                     rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, cov1, size=n_eval)])
y_eval = np.array([0]*n_eval + [1]*n_eval)

n_reps = 30
for n_per_class in [10, 20, 50, 200, 2000]:
    lda_accs, qda_accs = [], []
    for _ in range(n_reps):
        X_train = np.vstack([
            rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, cov0, size=n_per_class),
            rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, cov1, size=n_per_class),
        ])
        y_train = np.array([0]*n_per_class + [1]*n_per_class)
        lda_accs.append(LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_eval, y_eval))
        qda_accs.append(QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_eval, y_eval))
    print(n_per_class, round(np.mean(lda_accs), 4), round(np.mean(qda_accs), 4))
examples.explanation: The two classes have different covariance matrices (cov0 is isotropic, cov1 is larger and correlated), so QDA, which models per-class covariance, is the better-specified model and pulls ahead as n_per_class grows (about even at 50 per class, clearly ahead from 200). With only 10 or 20 examples per class, LDA wins, because QDA's extra covariance parameters, estimated from so little class-specific data, add more estimation noise than they remove modeling bias. The large fixed evaluation set (20,000 points per class) keeps evaluation noise low, and averaging over 30 training sets per size smooths out the luck of any one small sample, so the bias-variance tradeoff shows up in the averages instead of in one noisy accuracy number.

examples.title: LDA vs PCA as Dimensionality Reduction on the Same Data
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

iris = load_iris()
X, y = iris.data, iris.target

X_lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2).fit_transform(X, y)
X_pca = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)

for name, Z in [("LDA", X_lda), ("PCA", X_pca)]:
    means = np.array([Z[y == c].mean(axis=0) for c in np.unique(y)])
    within = np.mean([Z[y == c].std(axis=0).mean() for c in np.unique(y)])
    between = np.std(means, axis=0).mean()
    print(name, round(between / within, 3))
examples.explanation: `LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2).fit_transform(X, y)` needs `y`, while `PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)` does not use one (its `y=None` parameter exists only for pipeline compatibility). LDA's between/within separation ratio (3.128) is clearly higher than PCA's (2.253) on the same data reduced to the same number of dimensions, because LDA optimizes class separation using the labels, while PCA optimizes total variance and has no way to know whether a direction separates the three iris species. The ratio is a rough metric defined in this code, not a standard statistic.

misconceptions.description: LDA and QDA are just 'linear' and 'quadratic' flavors of logistic regression, differing only in the shape of decision boundary someone chose to fit.
misconceptions.clarification: LDA and QDA are generative models: they explicitly assume each class's features follow a multivariate Normal distribution and derive the classifier by inverting that assumption with Bayes' rule, and the linear-versus-quadratic shape of the boundary falls directly, mathematically out of whether the covariance matrix is shared across classes (LDA) or class-specific (QDA) -- it follows from a distributional assumption instead of being an independent design choice. Logistic regression, by contrast, is discriminative: it directly models the boundary between classes and makes no assumption about how the features are distributed within each class and arrives at a linear boundary for different reasons than LDA does. Two methods can produce the same-shaped boundary while resting on completely different foundations, and those foundations determine how each method fails: LDA/QDA degrade when the Normality assumption is badly violated, while logistic regression is comparatively indifferent to that particular assumption but can struggle when classes are not linearly (or, without added feature engineering, quadratically) separable at all.

misconceptions.description: QDA is strictly better than LDA because it's strictly more flexible and includes LDA as a special case, so there's no real reason to ever prefer the more restrictive model.
misconceptions.clarification: In the infinite-data limit this is true in principle -- with enough data, QDA can recover LDA's shared-covariance behavior if that's genuinely what the data looks like, and can do better if it isn't. But with realistic, finite training data, QDA pays for its added flexibility by estimating a full separate covariance matrix per class, using only that class's own examples, which is a noisier estimate than LDA's single covariance pooled across every class's examples at once. The demonstration above shows LDA outperforming QDA at small sample sizes per class (10, 20 examples) even though the true covariances differ between classes, with QDA only pulling ahead once there is enough data per class (about 50 and up here) to estimate its extra parameters reliably. It is a measured instance of the general rule that a more flexible model needs more data to earn back its flexibility.

exercises.prompt: Two classes are generated with the SAME covariance matrix but different means. A test point sits exactly halfway between the two class means. If you fit LDA and look at predict_proba for that point, what should the two class probabilities be, and why?
exercises.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
mean0, mean1 = np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.array([4.0, 4.0])
shared_cov = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])

X0 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, shared_cov, size=500)
X1 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, shared_cov, size=500)
X = np.vstack([X0, X1])
y = np.array([0]*500 + [1]*500)

lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(X, y)
midpoint = (mean0 + mean1) / 2
print(np.round(lda.predict_proba([midpoint]), 3))
hints: With equal covariance and equal class sizes (equal priors), what does symmetry alone tell you about a point exactly equidistant, in every sense, from both class means?

LDA's decision boundary passes through the point where the two classes' densities (and, with equal priors, their posteriors) are exactly tied -- is the midpoint of two equal-covariance class means exactly such a point?

The predicted probabilities for the two classes should each come out near 0.5, since the midpoint lies on the true decision boundary. The fitted boundary is estimated from a finite sample, though, so expect a small deviation.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints two probabilities near 0.5; with this seed the output is [[0.443 0.557]]. Because both classes share the same covariance matrix and have equal (500-vs-500) priors, the point halfway between the two class means lies, by symmetry, on the true linear decision boundary, the set of points where the two classes' posterior probabilities are tied. In theory neither class is favored. The fitted boundary is estimated from 500 points per class, so it lands slightly off the true midpoint and tilts the probabilities a little.
exercises.solutionExplanation: LDA's decision boundary is defined as the set of points where P(Y=0|X=x) equals P(Y=1|X=x). With a shared covariance matrix and equal class priors, this boundary is a hyperplane through the midpoint of the two class means (with the identity covariance used here it is the perpendicular bisector of the segment between them). The midpoint therefore lies on the true boundary, and predict_proba there should return probabilities near 0.5 each. Estimating the means and covariance from 500 points per class moves the fitted boundary slightly off the true one, which is why this run prints [[0.443 0.557]] instead of exactly 0.5. This follows from the linear-boundary derivation: with equal priors and a shared covariance, the boundary passes through the midpoint of the class means.

exercises.prompt: This code tries to fit QDA on a dataset where one class has only 2 examples in a 2-feature space, and it crashes with a linear algebra error. Explain what's actually wrong and fix it without simply deleting the small class.
exercises.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X0 = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, 0], [0, 1]], size=100)
X1 = rng.multivariate_normal([3, 3], [[1, 0], [0, 1]], size=2)   # only 2 samples, 2 features
X = np.vstack([X0, X1])
y = np.array([0]*100 + [1]*2)

qda = QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis()
qda.fit(X, y)   # raises: LinAlgError -- class 1's covariance matrix is not full rank
print(qda.predict([[3, 3], [0, 0]]))
hints: QDA needs to estimate a full, separate covariance matrix for every class -- how many data points does it actually have available for class 1, and how does that compare to the number of features (2)?

With only 2 samples in 2 dimensions, class 1's covariance matrix estimate is mathematically rank-deficient (singular) -- there isn't enough data in that class alone to pin down a full 2x2 covariance matrix, regardless of how much data the other class has.

QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis has a reg_param argument specifically for this situation -- it shrinks each per-class covariance estimate toward a better-conditioned matrix, which is a more principled fix here than throwing the small class's data away entirely.
exercises.solutionCode:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X0 = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, 0], [0, 1]], size=100)
X1 = rng.multivariate_normal([3, 3], [[1, 0], [0, 1]], size=2)
X = np.vstack([X0, X1])
y = np.array([0]*100 + [1]*2)

# reg_param shrinks each per-class covariance estimate, fixing the rank deficiency
qda = QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis(reg_param=0.3)
qda.fit(X, y)
print(qda.predict([[3, 3], [0, 0]]))   # [1, 0] -- correctly separates the two regions
print(qda.score(X, y))
exercises.solutionExplanation: QDA has to estimate a genuinely separate p-by-p covariance matrix for every class using only that class's own examples, and with only 2 samples in a 2-feature space, class 1's covariance estimate is rank-deficient (its rank is at most n-1=1, less than the 2 needed for a full-rank 2x2 matrix), which is what the LinAlgError reports, not a bug in the surrounding code. Recent scikit-learn versions raise this error; how rank deficiency is reported can vary between versions. Deleting the small class isn't a real fix -- it just avoids the classifier having to model that class at all. The `reg_param` argument to QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis regularizes each per-class covariance estimate by shrinking it toward a well-conditioned matrix, trading a small amount of bias for a covariance estimate that is invertible, which is QDA's built-in remedy for small classes. With reg_param=0.3 the fit succeeds and classifies both test points correctly.

assessments.prompt: Why does LDA's decision boundary come out linear specifically, in terms of the derivation from the class-conditional Normal densities?
options: Because LDA assumes every class shares the same covariance matrix.
Because LDA arbitrarily restricts itself to fitting a straight line to the data, regardless of any other modeling assumption.
Because LDA is fit using gradient descent on a linear loss function, similar to linear regression.
Because LDA only ever handles exactly two classes, and two classes can always be separated by a straight line.
assessments.explanation: With a shared Sigma across classes, the quadratic terms in the log-density-ratio between two classes are identical and cancel out, leaving a function linear in x, which defines a hyperplane boundary. The “Because LDA arbitrarily restricts itself to fitting…” option treats the linearity as an arbitrary restriction rather than a mathematical consequence of the shared-covariance assumption. The “Because LDA is fit using gradient descent…” option is false; LDA has a closed-form solution derived from Gaussian densities and Bayes' rule, not an iterative gradient-based fit. The “Because LDA only ever handles exactly two…” option is false; LDA generalizes to any number of classes, and linear separability with more than two classes is a property of the specific data, not an automatic guarantee.

assessments.prompt: In the bias-variance demonstration above, LDA outperforms QDA at 10-20 samples per class, even though the two classes' true covariance matrices genuinely differ. What does this illustrate?
options: LDA and QDA are mathematically identical algorithms, so any observed difference in accuracy is purely random noise.

LDA's shared-covariance assumption, while technically wrong for this data, produces a lower-variance estimate that generalizes better with very little per-class data; QDA's extra per-class covariance parameters need more data to be estimated reliably before its lower bias can actually pay off.
The result must be due to a coding error, since the more flexible, correctly-specified model (QDA) should always outperform the more restrictive one (LDA) regardless of sample size.
QDA is a fundamentally broken algorithm that should never be used in practice.
assessments.explanation: This is the bias-variance tradeoff: QDA's per-class covariance estimates, built from only that class's own small sample, are noisier than LDA's single pooled covariance estimate, so at small sample sizes the extra flexibility QDA offers costs more in variance than it gains in reduced bias, even though QDA's assumption matches the true generative process more closely. The “QDA is a fundamentally broken algorithm…” option overgeneralizes a small-sample result into a blanket claim; the same demonstration shows QDA pulling ahead once there's enough data per class. The “The result must be due…” option wrongly assumes flexibility always wins regardless of sample size, ignoring the estimation-variance cost of that flexibility. The “LDA and QDA are mathematically identical algorithms…” option is false; LDA and QDA make different modeling assumptions (shared versus per-class covariance) and are not mathematically identical.

assessments.prompt: How does LDA's use as a dimensionality-reduction technique fundamentally differ from PCA's, in terms of what each method's objective actually optimizes?
options: PCA requires labeled data while LDA does not, making LDA the more broadly applicable of the two techniques.

LDA and PCA both require the features to be classified into a fixed number of discrete bins before either can be applied, after which the two methods optimize exactly the same quantity on the binned data.
They optimize the identical objective; LDA is simply PCA restricted to exactly 2 output dimensions.
LDA maximizes the ratio of between-class variance to within-class variance using the labels y, while PCA maximizes total variance in the features with no reference to any label at all.
assessments.explanation: The distinction shows up numerically: LDA's `fit_transform(X, y)` explicitly uses the class labels to maximize a between-class-versus-within-class variance ratio (Fisher's criterion), producing a noticeably higher separation ratio on the iris dataset (3.128) than PCA's `fit_transform(X)` (2.253), which never sees y and only ever maximizes total variance in the raw features. The “They optimize the identical objective; LDA…” option wrongly equates two objectives that are provably different, as the differing separation ratios on identical data show. The “PCA requires labeled data while LDA does…” option reverses which method actually needs labels -- PCA is the one that works without them, not LDA. The “LDA and PCA both require the features…” option describes neither method accurately; both operate on continuous numeric feature vectors.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague, using the generative Gaussian assumption as the organizing idea, how to decide between LDA and QDA for a given classification problem, and why the choice is fundamentally a bias-variance tradeoff rather than a simple 'pick the more powerful model' decision.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both LDA and QDA model each class's features as coming from a multivariate Normal distribution and classify a new point using Bayes' rule, so the real question separating them is a single structural choice: does every class share one common covariance matrix (LDA), or does each class get its own, separately estimated covariance matrix (QDA)? That assumption determines the geometry of the decision boundary: a shared covariance makes the quadratic terms in the class-comparison math cancel out, leaving a boundary that's a straight hyperplane, while separate covariances leave those quadratic terms in place, producing curved, quadratic boundaries that can bend around each class's own actual shape. It is easy to assume QDA should always be preferred, since it is more expressive and can represent anything LDA can, but that ignores where its extra parameters come from: QDA has to estimate a full covariance matrix separately for every class, using only that one class's own training examples, whereas LDA pools every class's examples into a single shared covariance estimate. When any class has relatively few examples, QDA's per-class covariance estimates become noisy and unreliable even if the true covariances really do differ across classes, and a concrete comparison at small sample sizes (10-20 examples per class) shows LDA actually winning in exactly this regime, with QDA only pulling ahead once there's enough data per class -- 50 or more in that example -- to estimate its extra parameters reliably. The practical rule of thumb follows directly: reach for LDA by default, especially with limited data or many classes relative to sample size, and consider QDA specifically when you have good reason to believe the classes' covariance structures genuinely differ and you have enough data per class to estimate that structure without just adding noise.

concepts.title: Factor Analysis and Canonical Correlation Analysis
concepts.description: Factor Analysis models observed variables as linear combinations of a small number of unobserved latent factors plus independent per-variable noise, explicitly separating shared structure from idiosyncratic noise in a way PCA never does, while Canonical Correlation Analysis finds linear combinations of two entirely different variable sets that correlate with each other as strongly as possible -- both are direct conceptual ancestors of modern latent-representation and multi-modal-alignment ideas.
learningObjectives: Describe the Factor Analysis generative model: observed variables as linear combinations of latent factors plus independent, per-variable noise.
Contrast Factor Analysis's explicit noise model with PCA's lack of one, and explain concretely how that changes what each method actually recovers.
Fit a Factor Analysis model with sklearn.decomposition.FactorAnalysis and interpret its loading matrix and per-variable noise estimates.
Describe Canonical Correlation Analysis's objective: finding linear combinations of two different variable sets that are maximally correlated with each other.
Apply CCA to align two views or modalities of the same underlying phenomenon and interpret the resulting canonical correlation.

sections.heading: Factor Analysis: A Generative Model With an Explicit Noise Term
sections.body:
**Factor Analysis (FA)** assumes each observed feature vector x is generated as x = Lambda @ f + mu + epsilon, where f is a small vector of unobserved **latent factors** (assumed to follow a standard multivariate Normal distribution), Lambda is a matrix of **loadings** describing how strongly each observed variable depends on each latent factor, mu is the overall mean, and epsilon is per-variable noise, assumed independent across variables with its own variance for each one (so its covariance matrix Psi is diagonal -- no cross-variable noise correlation, only variable-specific noise magnitude). Under this model, the covariance of the observed variables works out to Sigma = Lambda @ Lambda^T + Psi: shared structure coming through the factors, contributed by Lambda @ Lambda^T, plus each variable's own idiosyncratic, independent noise variance sitting on the diagonal via Psi.

The classic motivating story for this model comes from psychometrics: imagine several different test scores -- vocabulary, arithmetic, spatial reasoning -- that all correlate with each other to some degree. FA hypothesizes that the correlation arises because all of these scores are, to varying degrees, reflections of a smaller number of unobserved latent traits (a general 'ability' factor, say), with each score also carrying its own measurement noise and test-specific quirks unrelated to the shared trait. Fitting FA (typically via maximum likelihood, often through the EM algorithm) means estimating Lambda and Psi from the observed covariance structure alone, without ever directly observing f.

sections.heading: Why the Noise Model Changes What Each Method Actually Recovers
sections.body:
PCA, by contrast, has no epsilon term at all: it decomposes total observed variance directly, with no explicit separation between 'variance shared with other variables' and 'variance that's just this one variable's own idiosyncratic noise.' This changes what each method recovers. PCA's first component is the direction with the most *total* variance, whether that variance is shared structure or just one variable being noisy. If one observed variable happens to have much larger idiosyncratic variance than the others, PCA's first component can end up dominated by that single noisy variable, even though it shares comparatively little with everything else.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import FactorAnalysis, PCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 2000
factor = rng.normal(size=n)                       # one shared latent factor

loadings = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6])
noise_sd = np.array([0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 3.0])         # variable 4 is much noisier than the rest

X = np.outer(factor, loadings) + rng.normal(size=(n, 4)) * noise_sd

fa = FactorAnalysis(n_components=1, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("FA loadings:       ", np.round(fa.components_[0], 3))        # [0.897 0.808 0.689 0.596]
print("FA noise variance: ", np.round(fa.noise_variance_, 3))       # [0.096 0.085 0.088 8.873]

pca = PCA(n_components=1).fit(X)
print("PCA first component:", np.round(pca.components_[0], 3))       # [0.072 0.065 0.057 0.994]
print("PCA explained var ratio:", np.round(pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 3))   # [0.816]
```

FA recovers loadings close to the true generating values (0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6) and attributes almost all of variable 4's variance to noise (noise_variance_ of 8.873, close to the true noise_sd[3]^2 = 9.0) rather than to the shared factor, which is the separation the model is designed to make. PCA's first component, by contrast, is almost entirely variable 4 (a loading of 0.994, versus about 0.06-0.07 for the other three), because variable 4's noise variance (about 9.2 in this sample, nearly all of it unshared noise) outweighs everything else, and PCA cannot tell that this variance is idiosyncratic rather than shared signal. FA's explicit Psi term lets it see past one noisy variable's raw variance to the shared structure underneath.

sections.heading: Canonical Correlation Analysis: Correlating Two Different Views of the Same Phenomenon
sections.body:
**Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA)** answers a different question: given two separate sets of variables, X (p-dimensional) and Y (q-dimensional), measured on the same set of n samples -- two different 'views' of the same underlying units -- which linear combination a^T X of the first view's variables and which linear combination b^T Y of the second view's variables are as correlated with *each other* as possible? Unlike PCA (which only ever looks within one variable set for directions of maximum internal variance) or ordinary pairwise correlation (which only ever compares one specific column against another specific column), CCA searches over every possible linear combination of each entire variable set simultaneously, looking for the pairing that maximizes cross-set correlation.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import CCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = 2000
shared = rng.normal(size=n)   # underlying signal present in both views, but noisily so in each

X = np.column_stack([shared + rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=n),
                      shared + rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=n)])   # view 1, e.g. text-embedding channels
Y = np.column_stack([shared + rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=n),
                      shared + rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=n)])   # view 2, e.g. image-embedding channels

print("raw single-column correlations, all individually weak:")
for i in range(2):
    for j in range(2):
        print(f"  X[:,{i}] vs Y[:,{j}]: {np.corrcoef(X[:, i], Y[:, j])[0, 1]:.3f}")

cca = CCA(n_components=1).fit(X, Y)
X_c, Y_c = cca.transform(X, Y)
canonical_corr = np.corrcoef(X_c[:, 0], Y_c[:, 0])[0, 1]
print("canonical correlation (best combination of both columns per view):", round(canonical_corr, 4))
```

Every individual column-to-column correlation between the two views comes out weak here (around 0.27-0.31), because each individual channel is a noisy reflection of the shared signal on its own. But CCA's optimal linear combination of both columns in each view -- roughly an even blend of the two channels in X and the two in Y, since averaging cancels some of the independent per-channel noise -- achieves a higher canonical correlation of about 0.448, recovering more of the shared signal than any single column pair can. (The population value for this setup is 4/8.5, about 0.47; 0.448 is the sample estimate.) This is the sense in which CCA 'aligns' two representations of the same phenomenon: it finds the combination of each entire view that best exposes the shared structure, instead of comparing one column to another.

sections.heading: Concrete Use Cases, and the Line Forward to Modern Representation Learning
sections.body:
Factor Analysis fits the psychometric, latent-trait setting it was built for: survey scales, personality inventories, or standardized test batteries where a handful of noisy, imperfect measurements are believed to reflect a smaller number of unobserved traits, and where you want to separate the shared trait signal from each measurement's own noise level. PCA is not designed for this and, as shown above, can get it wrong when noise levels differ substantially across variables.

CCA suits any situation with two different measurement systems, or 'views,' of the same underlying units that you want to relate to each other without picking one specific column from each side to compare by hand: aligning two different sensor modalities reading the same physical process, aligning two different feature representations of the same documents (say, a bag-of-words representation and a topic-model representation), or, in a more modern framing, aligning embeddings of the same concept produced by two different encoders -- one trained on text, one trained on images -- to find the shared, cross-modal structure connecting them, discovering which combination of dimensions in each encoder's output space corresponds to the same real-world signal.

Both methods are also conceptual ancestors of ideas common in modern representation learning. Factor Analysis's idea that high-dimensional observations are a noisy reflection of a few latent factors is the intuition behind a learned embedding space or a variational autoencoder's latent code, fit with far more flexible, usually nonlinear machinery than FA's linear generative model. CCA's idea that two views of the same phenomenon can be related through the linear combinations of each that correlate most strongly is the intuition behind multimodal embedding alignment (matching text and image embeddings of the same concept in a shared space), with a neural network trained on a contrastive objective in place of CCA's linear projections. Seeing the classical linear versions first makes the deep-learning versions less mysterious.

examples.title: Factor Analysis Recovering True Loadings and Noise Levels
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import FactorAnalysis

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 2000
factor = rng.normal(size=n)

loadings = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6])
noise_sd = np.array([0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 3.0])

X = np.outer(factor, loadings) + rng.normal(size=(n, 4)) * noise_sd

fa = FactorAnalysis(n_components=1, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("recovered loadings:", np.round(fa.components_[0], 3))
print("recovered noise variance:", np.round(fa.noise_variance_, 3))
print("true noise variance was:", np.round(noise_sd ** 2, 3))
examples.explanation: The recovered loadings (about 0.897, 0.808, 0.689, 0.596) are close to the true generating loadings (0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6), and the recovered per-variable noise variances (about 0.096, 0.085, 0.088, 8.873) closely track the true squared noise standard deviations (0.09, 0.09, 0.09, 9.0) -- FA correctly identifies that the fourth variable's variance is overwhelmingly noise rather than shared signal, which is the separation its explicit Psi term is built to make. `fa.components_` holds the loadings matrix Lambda (transposed to match sklearn's convention), and `fa.noise_variance_` holds the diagonal of Psi directly, giving a per-variable readout of how much of each observed variable's variance is idiosyncratic rather than shared with the latent factor.

examples.title: PCA Getting Hijacked by One Noisy Variable Where FA Does Not
examples.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import numpy as np

# fragment: X, loadings and noise_sd come from the Factor Analysis example above
pca = PCA(n_components=1).fit(X)
print("PCA first component weights:", np.round(pca.components_[0], 3))
print("PCA explained variance ratio:", np.round(pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 3))
examples.explanation: PCA's first component comes out at roughly [0.072, 0.065, 0.057, 0.994] -- almost entirely the fourth variable, the one built with ten times the noise standard deviation of the others. PCA is not malfunctioning: it maximizes captured total variance, and variable 4's noise is the largest source of variance in this dataset. The problem is interpretation. Someone reading this PCA result could wrongly conclude that variable 4 is the most informative variable, when it shares the least structure with the others. FA's explicit noise model guards against that misreading.

examples.title: CCA Recovering Shared Structure Across Two Noisy Views
examples.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import CCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = 2000
shared = rng.normal(size=n)

X = np.column_stack([shared + rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=n),
                      shared + rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=n)])
Y = np.column_stack([shared + rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=n),
                      shared + rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=n)])

cca = CCA(n_components=1).fit(X, Y)
X_c, Y_c = cca.transform(X, Y)
print("canonical correlation:", round(np.corrcoef(X_c[:, 0], Y_c[:, 0])[0, 1], 4))
print("X weights:", np.round(cca.x_weights_.ravel(), 3))
print("Y weights:", np.round(cca.y_weights_.ravel(), 3))
examples.explanation: The canonical correlation of about 0.448 is higher than any individual raw column-to-column correlation between the two views (all in the 0.27-0.31 range, computed in the explanation above), because CCA's `x_weights_` (about [0.773, 0.635]) and `y_weights_` (about [0.676, 0.737]) combine both noisy channels within each view into a single direction that averages out some of each channel's independent noise, more cleanly exposing the shared signal both views were generated from. CCA does not look at one column from each side in isolation; it searches over combinations of the *entire* variable set on each side for the pairing that correlates best across the two views.

misconceptions.description: Factor Analysis and PCA are basically the same algorithm with two different names, so it doesn't matter much which one you reach for.
misconceptions.clarification: PCA has no noise model at all -- it decomposes total observed variance directly and treats all of it as potentially meaningful, with no built-in way to separate variance shared across variables from variance that's just one particular variable's own idiosyncratic noise. Factor Analysis explicitly includes a diagonal noise covariance Psi, one independent noise variance per observed variable, and estimates it separately from the shared-factor loadings Lambda. The demonstration above shows the consequence: when one variable has much higher idiosyncratic noise than the others, PCA's first component is dominated by that variable's raw variance, while FA isolates that noise into Psi and recovers loadings close to the true shared-factor structure. The two coincide only in a special case, probabilistic PCA, where every variable has the same isotropic noise level, which is not this example.

misconceptions.description: CCA finds the features that are individually most important or most variable within each dataset, similar in spirit to picking the top features by variance or by feature selection.
misconceptions.clarification: CCA ignores how much variance a feature has within its own view, or how 'important' it seems in isolation; its objective is finding linear combinations across the two views that correlate with *each other* as strongly as possible. A feature could have enormous variance within its own dataset and contribute essentially nothing to the top canonical correlation if it has no relationship to anything in the other view, and, symmetrically, a feature with modest variance on its own could be weighted heavily by CCA if it happens to be the one that best tracks the signal in the other view. In the worked example both channels of each view carry the same signal at the same noise level, so CCA blends them (weights of about 0.77 and 0.64 in X, 0.68 and 0.74 in Y) instead of picking one: its target is the relationship between the two sets, not a ranking of features within either set.

exercises.prompt: Four variables share one latent factor with loadings [0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6], but variable 4 has ten times the noise standard deviation of the other three. Which method's first component/loading vector will end up dominated by variable 4 -- PCA's or Factor Analysis's -- and roughly what will each look like?
exercises.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import FactorAnalysis, PCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 2000
factor = rng.normal(size=n)
loadings = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6])
noise_sd = np.array([0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 3.0])
X = np.outer(factor, loadings) + rng.normal(size=(n, 4)) * noise_sd

fa = FactorAnalysis(n_components=1, random_state=0).fit(X)
pca = PCA(n_components=1).fit(X)
print("FA loadings: ", np.round(fa.components_[0], 2))
print("PCA loadings:", np.round(pca.components_[0], 2))
hints: Which method's objective is 'capture the most total variance,' with no distinction between shared and idiosyncratic variance -- and which variable in this setup has by far the most total variance, purely from its noise?

Factor Analysis explicitly models a separate noise variance per variable (Psi) and is specifically trying to separate that noise out from genuine shared structure -- what should that let it recover instead of getting distracted by the noisy variable?
Expect PCA's loading vector to be dominated by a single large weight on variable 4, and FA's loading vector to instead track the true relative loadings [0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6] reasonably closely.
exercises.expectedAnswer: PCA's first component is dominated by variable 4 (something like [0.07, 0.07, 0.06, 0.99]) purely because it has the largest total variance, most of which is noise, not shared signal. Factor Analysis's loadings instead come out close to the true generating loadings, something like [0.90, 0.81, 0.69, 0.60], because FA explicitly separates each variable's idiosyncratic noise into a separate parameter (noise_variance_) rather than letting it pollute the shared-structure estimate.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Variable 4 was constructed with a noise standard deviation of 3.0, ten times larger than the other three variables' 0.3, giving it, by far, the largest total variance in the dataset -- most of that variance is pure noise, unrelated to the shared factor, but PCA has no mechanism to distinguish 'variance because this variable is noisy' from 'variance because this variable strongly reflects real shared structure,' so its first component ends up almost entirely aligned with variable 4 (loading around 0.99, versus around 0.06-0.07 for the rest). Factor Analysis explicitly models a separate noise variance per observed variable via Psi, and fitting the model correctly attributes most of variable 4's variance to that noise term rather than to the shared factor, leaving FA's loadings vector free to track the true underlying loadings [0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6] reasonably closely instead of being distorted by one variable's noise level.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to use CCA to find the strongest linear relationship between a 3-column view X and a 2-column view Y, but it crashes. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import CCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
shared = rng.normal(size=500)
X = np.column_stack([shared + rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=500) for _ in range(3)])
Y = np.column_stack([shared + rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=500) for _ in range(2)])

cca = CCA(n_components=3)   # bug is here
cca.fit(X, Y)
X_c, Y_c = cca.transform(X, Y)
print(X_c.shape, Y_c.shape)
hints: The number of canonical components CCA can extract is capped by the SMALLER of the two views' dimensionalities -- how many columns does Y actually have?

n_components=3 asks CCA to find 3 mutually orthogonal canonical directions in Y's space, but Y only has 2 columns/dimensions to begin with -- there simply aren't 3 independent directions available there.
Set n_components to at most min(X.shape[1], Y.shape[1]) -- here, min(3, 2) = 2 -- rather than picking a number based only on one of the two views.
exercises.solutionCode:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import CCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
shared = rng.normal(size=500)
X = np.column_stack([shared + rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=500) for _ in range(3)])
Y = np.column_stack([shared + rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=500) for _ in range(2)])

n_components = min(X.shape[1], Y.shape[1])   # capped by the smaller view: 2
cca = CCA(n_components=n_components)
cca.fit(X, Y)
X_c, Y_c = cca.transform(X, Y)
print(X_c.shape, Y_c.shape)   # (500, 2) (500, 2)
exercises.solutionExplanation: CCA finds pairs of linear combinations, one from each view, and the number of such pairs it can extract is limited by whichever view has fewer dimensions -- with only 2 columns, Y simply cannot supply 3 mutually orthogonal canonical directions, no matter how many columns X has. Requesting n_components=3 when Y only has 2 columns asks for more independent directions than the smaller view can possibly provide, which is exactly what raises the error. Setting n_components to min(X.shape[1], Y.shape[1]) -- 2 in this case -- respects that structural limit and lets CCA fit and transform successfully, returning transformed matrices with exactly that many columns for both views.

assessments.prompt: What is the key structural difference between Factor Analysis's generative model and PCA that explains why FA can correctly handle a variable with unusually high idiosyncratic noise while PCA cannot?
options: FA uses a different linear algebra library internally, which happens to be more numerically robust to noisy variables.
PCA requires the data to be centered first, while FA does not, and this centering step is what causes PCA's sensitivity to noisy variables.
FA can only be applied to exactly one latent factor at a time, forcing it to ignore noisy variables by construction.

FA explicitly includes a per-variable noise term (a diagonal noise covariance Psi) separate from the shared-factor structure, while PCA decomposes total variance directly with no such separation, so a variable's raw noise variance can dominate PCA's components but gets isolated into Psi by FA.
assessments.explanation: The worked comparison above shows this: FA's model explicitly separates Sigma into Lambda @ Lambda^T (shared structure) plus Psi (independent, per-variable noise), and fitting it correctly attributes a noisy variable's variance mostly to Psi, recovering loadings close to the true values; PCA has no equivalent separation and its first component gets dominated by whichever variable has the largest total variance, regardless of whether that variance is meaningful or just noise. The “FA uses a different linear algebra library…” option misattributes the difference to implementation rather than to the models' mathematical structure. The “FA can only be applied to exactly…” option is false; FA can be fit with any number of latent factors, chosen by the analyst, not fixed at one. The “PCA requires the data to be centered…” option is a red herring -- both PCA and FA rely on properly centered data, and centering is not what causes PCA's noise sensitivity.

assessments.prompt: What does Canonical Correlation Analysis specifically search for, given two variable sets X and Y measured on the same samples?
options: The single column in X and the single column in Y that have the highest ordinary Pearson correlation with each other across all of the samples.
A classification boundary that best separates X's samples from Y's samples.
A linear combination of all of X's variables and a linear combination of all of Y's variables that are as correlated with each other as possible.
The principal components of X and Y computed separately, then compared afterward for similarity.
assessments.explanation: CCA's objective is to search over every possible linear combination of X's variables together with every possible linear combination of Y's variables, for the specific pair that maximizes the correlation between the two resulting combined scores -- not to check individual column pairs one at a time, and not to run two separate, unrelated analyses. The “The single column in X…” option describes ordinary pairwise correlation, which the concept's worked example shows can be much weaker than the true cross-view relationship CCA recovers by combining multiple columns per view. The “The principal components of X and Y…” option describes running PCA twice with no cross-view objective at all, missing CCA's defining cross-correlation goal entirely. The “A classification boundary that best separates X's…” option describes a classification task, unrelated to CCA's actual correlation-maximization objective.

assessments.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches each technique to the concrete use case the concept associates with it?
options: Factor Analysis and CCA are interchangeable and are associated with the exact same use cases in the concept.

Factor Analysis for modeling a latent trait like 'ability' behind several correlated, individually noisy test scores; CCA for finding the shared structure between two different views or modalities of the same underlying phenomenon.

Factor Analysis for aligning two different modalities' embeddings of the same concept; CCA for modeling a latent trait like 'ability' behind several correlated test scores, with both methods requiring labels for every sample before they can be fitted at all.
Factor Analysis is used exclusively for classification tasks, and CCA is used exclusively for regression tasks.
assessments.explanation: FA is associated with the classic psychometric scenario -- several noisy, correlated observed measurements (test scores) reflecting a smaller number of genuinely unobserved latent traits, with FA explicitly separating shared trait signal from each measurement's own noise -- and associates CCA with relating two structurally different variable sets or 'views' of the same underlying units, such as two sensor modalities or two different embedding spaces of the same concept. The “Factor Analysis for aligning two different modalities'…” option swaps the two use cases entirely. The “Factor Analysis and CCA are interchangeable…” option denies the distinction between the two methods. The “Factor Analysis is used exclusively for classification…” option mischaracterizes both methods, neither of which is a classification or regression technique in the way described.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague why Factor Analysis and Canonical Correlation Analysis are worth understanding as conceptual ancestors of modern representation-learning ideas, even though most current ML systems don't use either technique directly by name.
assessments.modelAnswer: Factor Analysis's core assumption is that the high-dimensional, noisy data you actually observe is a reflection of a much smaller number of genuinely meaningful latent factors, plus independent noise specific to each observed measurement -- and that is exactly the same intuition behind a learned embedding space or a variational autoencoder's latent code in modern deep learning: a compact latent representation is assumed to capture the real underlying structure, while the messy, high-dimensional observed data (pixels, tokens, raw sensor readings) is treated as a noisy rendering of that latent structure. The difference is almost entirely one of machinery rather than idea -- FA fits a linear generative model with Gaussian assumptions via maximum likelihood, while a modern autoencoder fits a nonlinear generative model with a neural network via gradient descent, but the underlying claim, that observed high-dimensional data is a corrupted view of a lower-dimensional true signal, is the same claim in both cases. Canonical Correlation Analysis's core idea, that two different views of the same underlying phenomenon can be related by finding the linear combination of each view that correlates most strongly with the other, is exactly the intuition behind modern multi-modal embedding alignment: mapping text and image embeddings of the same concept into a shared space where corresponding concepts end up close together, or aligning representations from two different sensors or encoders describing the same real-world process. Contrastive learning objectives used to train today's multi-modal models are, at a conceptual level, a highly flexible, nonlinear, large-scale descendant of exactly the cross-view correlation-maximization goal CCA solves in closed form for the linear case. Understanding the classical, fully worked-out linear versions of these ideas first gives you a concrete, checkable mental model -- loadings, noise variances, canonical correlations you can compute by hand on small examples -- that makes the more complex, nonlinear, and much larger-scale modern systems built on the same underlying intuition considerably less mysterious to reason about.
